Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/11/whos-donating-to-the-billionaire-backed-group-has-raised-almost-300-million-to-fight-the-wealth-tax/) showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.

Endorsement: California hasn’t even bothered to study its existing public financing programs. No on Prop 4
Proposition 4 would overturn California’s ban on public financing of campaigns but does not include key guardrails.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
There’s no excuse for Prop 4’s backers’ failure to do this homework, given that voters rejected efforts to lift California’s ban on public campaign financing in 2000 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html), 2006 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2006/89_11_2006.htm) and 2010 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2010/15_06_2010.aspx).
We encourage you to vote no again.

Endorsement: California hasn’t even bothered to study its existing public financing programs. No on Prop 4
Proposition 4 would overturn California’s ban on public financing of campaigns but does not include key guardrails.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?

That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.

Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

Endorsement: California hasn’t even bothered to study its existing public financing programs. No on Prop 4
Proposition 4 would overturn California’s ban on public financing of campaigns but does not include key guardrails.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

Endorsement: California hasn’t even bothered to study its existing public financing programs. No on Prop 4
Proposition 4 would overturn California’s ban on public financing of campaigns but does not include key guardrails.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

Good. This is a substantive legal concern. Prop 4's subdivision (f) allows increased expenditure limits based on "net supportive funds" of other candidates and independent expenditures — that's essentially a trigger mechanism similar to Arizona's, which was struck down in Bennett. However, subdivision (i) allows the Legislature to amend subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) by simple majority statute, so this is fixable.

But there's a more important point: even if (f) is struck down, the rest of the measure (lifting the ban) would remain. And the LAO analysis doesn't flag constitutional concerns.

Now let me look at:
1. Who funded Yes on 4 vs No on 4 (money behind the measure).
2. The San Diego Union-Tribune's editorial (the strongest "no" case).
3. Sacramento Bee's yes case.
4. Also, does the measure have any provision that might allow state legislators to create their own public financing? Yes — "state or a local governmental entity establishes a dedicated fund for this purpose by statute." So the Legislature could self-fund. That's a legitimate concern (conflict of interest). Though they'd need a 2/3 vote? Actually, creating a dedicated fund by statute — appropriations require majority, but a tax increase requires 2/3. There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

Good. This is a substantive legal concern. Prop 4's subdivision (f) allows increased expenditure limits based on "net supportive funds" of other candidates and independent expenditures — that's essentially a trigger mechanism similar to Arizona's, which was struck down in Bennett. However, subdivision (i) allows the Legislature to amend subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) by simple majority statute, so this is fixable.

But there's a more important point: even if (f) is struck down, the rest of the measure (lifting the ban) would remain. And the LAO analysis doesn't flag constitutional concerns.

Now let me look at:
1. Who funded Yes on 4 vs No on 4 (money behind the measure).
2. The San Diego Union-Tribune's editorial (the strongest "no" case).
3. Sacramento Bee's yes case.
4. Also, does the measure have any provision that might allow state legislators to create their own public financing? Yes — "state or a local governmental entity establishes a dedicated fund for this purpose by statute." So the Legislature could self-fund. That's a legitimate concern (conflict of interest). Though they'd need a 2/3 vote? Actually, creating a dedicated fund by statute — appropriations require majority, but a tax increase requires 2/3. Also, under Prop 4, amending remaining subdivisions requires compliance with 81012(b) = 2/3 vote.

5. Important: What about the "county political party committees" claim? The opponents claim Prop 4 allows public financing of candidates for county central committees. Let me check — Section 85300 applies to "public officer" and "candidate" for "elective office." County central committee members are elected partisan party positions — arguably "elective office." That's a real if minor drafting sloppiness.

Let me now look at money, and the SDUT editorial and Sacramento Bee editorial. Also let me check the Yes campaign's funders and whether it's dominated by particular interests.

Also check whether there is a fiscal estimate for local costs (Scott Alexander said ~$75 million in extra local taxes).

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

2026 California Prop 4 guide: "Public financing" measure would let state and local governments give candidates public money for their campaigns
Proposition 4 repeals the 1988 ban that keeps the state, counties and most cities from funding campaigns. It creates no program itself; any government that wants one would set the amounts, under rules on spending limits, small-donor support and money for schools, roads and public safety.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 18, 2026

California's Proposition 4 is asking voters whether the state and local governments may fund candidates' campaigns with public money.
Proposition 4 would repeal the California law that bars the state, counties and most cities from giving candidates public money for their campaigns, a ban voters approved in 1988.
It would not create a public financing program or spend money on any campaign. It would let the state and local governments build their own programs, under conditions written into the measure: candidates who take public funds must accept spending limits and show broad support in their district, typically through small donations, and no money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety can be used. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the state's direct cost at "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions, and says the cost of any program a government chooses to create "could be significant." The measure also raises the maximum fine for illegal campaign contributions from foreign sources.
California Proposition 4 is the fourth statewide attempt to lift the 1988 public campaign financing ban, after measures in 2000, 2006 and 2010 drew between 25.7% and 42.7% yes. Prop 4, the California Fair Elections Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/) placed on the ballot by SB 42, which Senator Tom Umberg wrote and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on October 2, 2025. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and one of three that change how California runs elections, alongside Proposition 5 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/california-proposition-5-2026/)'s recall changes and Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/)'s voter ID rules. California voters have turned down three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban, in 2000, 2006 and 2010, each of which also created a program; this is the first to ask only whether the ban should go. PPIC's September survey found 42% yes and 53% no, and UC Berkeley's found 35% on each side. Almost no money has been raised on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, the 1988 ban and the court fight over an earlier attempt to lift it, the cities that already fund campaigns, the cost, the arguments and the polling.

This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 4 replaces California's ban on public campaign funds with conditions for any future program:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf) rewrites Government Code section 85300, the one-sentence ban in the Political Reform Act. Today that section says a public officer "shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office." Prop 4 keeps the prohibition only for funds "earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety," which opens every other public source to a program a government chooses to create by statute, ordinance or charter.
It then sets the ground rules. Candidates "shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds." The measure defines strict criteria as requirements that make candidates "demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents." A program that counts small donors cannot require any donor to give more than $10 to be counted, and it cannot require candidates to collect signatures or reach a total dollar amount above $10 per contributor. Programs may not "discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent."
Three uses of the money are banned outright. Public funds cannot pay legal defense fees or fines, and no candidate can use them to repay a personal loan to their own campaign. A candidate who takes public funds also cannot repay such a loan from any source once the campaign ends.
The measure sets no dollar amounts. It does not say how much a candidate can receive, what a match would be or how high a spending limit must be; those are left to each statute, ordinance or charter. It does cap one thing: a program may raise a participating candidate's spending limit when opponents or outside groups outspend them, but only up to a formula in the text, the highest "net supportive funds" of any other candidate in the race plus outside spending against the participating candidate, minus outside spending for them.

2026 California Prop 4 guide: "Public financing" measure would let state and local governments give candidates public money for their campaigns
Proposition 4 repeals the 1988 ban that keeps the state, counties and most cities from funding campaigns. It creates no program itself; any government that wants one would set the amounts, under rules on spending limits, small-donor support and money for schools, roads and public safety.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 18, 2026

California's Proposition 4 is asking voters whether the state and local governments may fund candidates' campaigns with public money.
Proposition 4 would repeal the California law that bars the state, counties and most cities from giving candidates public money for their campaigns, a ban voters approved in 1988.
It would not create a public financing program or spend money on any campaign. It would let the state and local governments build their own programs, under conditions written into the measure: candidates who take public funds must accept spending limits and show broad support in their district, typically through small donations, and no money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety can be used. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the state's direct cost at "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions, and says the cost of any program a government chooses to create "could be significant." The measure also raises the maximum fine for illegal campaign contributions from foreign sources.
California Proposition 4 is the fourth statewide attempt to lift the 1988 public campaign financing ban, after measures in 2000, 2006 and 2010 drew between 25.7% and 42.7% yes. Prop 4, the California Fair Elections Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/) placed on the ballot by SB 42, which Senator Tom Umberg wrote and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on October 2, 2025. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and one of three that change how California runs elections, alongside Proposition 5 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/california-proposition-5-2026/)'s recall changes and Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/)'s voter ID rules. California voters have turned down three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban, in 2000, 2006 and 2010, each of which also created a program; this is the first to ask only whether the ban should go. PPIC's September survey found 42% yes and 53% no, and UC Berkeley's found 35% on each side. Almost no money has been raised on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, the 1988 ban and the court fight over an earlier attempt to lift it, the cities that already fund campaigns, the cost, the arguments and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 4 replaces California's ban on public campaign funds with conditions for any future program:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf) rewrites Government Code section 85300, the one-sentence ban in the Political Reform Act. Today that section says a public officer "shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office." Prop 4 keeps the prohibition only for funds "earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety," which opens every other public source to a program a government chooses to create by statute, ordinance or charter.
It then sets the ground rules. Candidates "shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds." The measure defines strict criteria as requirements that make candidates "demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents." A program that counts small donors cannot require any donor to give more than $10 to be counted, and it cannot require candidates to collect signatures or reach a total dollar amount above $10 per contributor. Programs may not "discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent."
Three uses of the money are banned outright. Public funds cannot pay legal defense fees or fines, and no candidate can use them to repay a personal loan to their own campaign. A candidate who takes public funds also cannot repay such a loan from any source once the campaign ends.

2026 California Prop 4 guide: "Public financing" measure would let state and local governments give candidates public money for their campaigns
Proposition 4 repeals the 1988 ban that keeps the state, counties and most cities from funding campaigns. It creates no program itself; any government that wants one would set the amounts, under rules on spending limits, small-donor support and money for schools, roads and public safety.
by

Updated

California's Proposition 4 is asking voters whether the state and local governments may fund candidates' campaigns with public money.
Proposition 4 would repeal the California law that bars the state, counties and most cities from giving candidates public money for their campaigns, a ban voters approved in 1988.
It would not create a public financing program or spend money on any campaign. It would let the state and local governments build their own programs, under conditions written into the measure: candidates who take public funds must accept spending limits and show broad support in their district, typically through small donations, and no money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety can be used. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the state's direct cost at "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions, and says the cost of any program a government chooses to create "could be significant." The measure also raises the maximum fine for illegal campaign contributions from foreign sources.
California Proposition 4 is the fourth statewide attempt to lift the 1988 public campaign financing ban, after measures in 2000, 2006 and 2010 drew between 25.7% and 42.7% yes. Prop 4, the California Fair Elections Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/) placed on the ballot by SB 42, which Senator Tom Umberg wrote and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on October 2, 2025. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and one of three that change how California runs elections, alongside Proposition 5 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/california-proposition-5-2026/)'s recall changes and Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/)'s voter ID rules. California voters have turned down three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban, in 2000, 2006 and 2010, each of which also created a program; this is the first to ask only whether the ban should go. PPIC's September survey found 42% yes and 53% no, and UC Berkeley's found 35% on each side. Almost no money has been raised on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, the 1988 ban and the court fight over an earlier attempt to lift it, the cities that already fund campaigns, the cost, the arguments and the polling.

The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf) rewrites Government Code section 85300, the one-sentence ban in the Political Reform Act. Today that section says a public officer "shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office." Prop 4 keeps the prohibition only for funds "earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety," which opens every other public source to a program a government chooses to create by statute, ordinance or charter.
It then sets the ground rules. Candidates "shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds." The measure defines strict criteria as requirements that make candidates "demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents." A program that counts small donors cannot require any donor to give more than $10 to be counted, and it cannot require candidates to collect signatures or reach a total dollar amount above $10 per contributor. Programs may not "discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent."
Three uses of the money are banned outright. Public funds cannot pay legal defense fees or fines, and no candidate can use them to repay a personal loan to their own campaign. A candidate who takes public funds also cannot repay such a loan from any source once the campaign ends.
The measure sets no dollar amounts. It does not say how much a candidate can receive, what a match would be or how high a spending limit must be; those are left to each statute, ordinance or charter. 2026 California Prop 4 guide: "Public financing" measure would let state and local governments give candidates public money for their campaigns
Proposition 4 repeals the 1988 ban that keeps the state, counties and most cities from funding campaigns. It creates no program itself; any government that wants one would set the amounts, under rules on spending limits, small-donor support and money for schools, roads and public safety.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 18, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California's Proposition 4 is asking voters whether the state and local governments may fund candidates' campaigns with public money.
Proposition 4 would repeal the California law that bars the state, counties and most cities from giving candidates public money for their campaigns, a ban voters approved in 1988.
It would not create a public financing program or spend money on any campaign. It would let the state and local governments build their own programs, under conditions written into the measure: candidates who take public funds must accept spending limits and show broad support in their district, typically through small donations, and no money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety can be used. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the state's direct cost at "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions, and says the cost of any program a government chooses to create "could be significant." The measure also raises the maximum fine for illegal campaign contributions from foreign sources.
California Proposition 4 is the fourth statewide attempt to lift the 1988 public campaign financing ban, after measures in 2000, 2006 and 2010 drew between 25.7% and 42.7% yes. Prop 4, the California Fair Elections Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/) placed on the ballot by SB 42, which Senator Tom Umberg wrote and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on October 2, 2025. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and one of three that change how California runs elections, alongside Proposition 5 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/california-proposition-5-2026/)'s recall changes and Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/)'s voter ID rules. California voters have turned down three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban, in 2000, 2006 and 2010, each of which also created a program; this is the first to ask only whether the ban should go. PPIC's September survey found 42% yes and 53% no, and UC Berkeley's found 35% on each side. Almost no money has been raised on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, the 1988 ban and the court fight over an earlier attempt to lift it, the cities that already fund campaigns, the cost, the arguments and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 4 replaces California's ban on public campaign funds with conditions for any future program:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf) rewrites Government Code section 85300, the one-sentence ban in the Political Reform Act. Today that section says a public officer "shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office." Prop 4 keeps the prohibition only for funds "earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety," which opens every other public source to a program a government chooses to create by statute, ordinance or charter.
It then sets the ground rules. Candidates "shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds." The measure defines strict criteria as requirements that make candidates "demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents." A program that counts small donors cannot require any donor to give more than $10 to be counted, and it cannot require candidates to collect signatures or reach a total dollar amount above $10 per contributor. Programs may not "discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent."
Three uses of the money are banned outright. Public funds cannot pay legal defense fees or fines, and no candidate can use them to repay a personal loan to their own campaign. A candidate who takes public funds also cannot repay such a loan from any source once the campaign ends.
The measure sets no dollar amounts. It does not say how much a candidate can receive, what a match would be or how high a spending limit must be; those are left to each statute, ordinance or charter. It does cap one thing: a program may raise a participating candidate's spending limit when opponents or outside groups outspend them, but only up to a formula in the text, the highest "net supportive funds" of any other candidate in the race plus outside spending against the participating candidate, minus outside spending for them.
