Now I have a very complete picture. Let me also verify one more critical thing: the claim in the "Against" argument that Prop 4 "allows special interest money in politics" — i.e., candidates could take public funds AND big private contributions. Let me verify whether the measure requires participating candidates to limit/reject large contributions. Looking at the text: no explicit prohibition on also raising private contributions. But participating candidates must accept expenditure limits, which effectively caps total spending. In practice, matching-fund programs (like LA/SF) allow private contributions subject to contribution limits, and matching amplifies small ones. That's standard for the "small-donor matching" model — which is precisely the design that has the best evidence (NYC, LA per the 2017 study, though the study says LA's design was less effective than NYC's).

So the "No" argument that it "allows special interest money" is technically true but somewhat misleading: all public financing models except full-grant "clean elections" models allow continued private contributions. The measure's design (small-dollar qualifying + expenditure limits) is the matching-fund model.

Another key question: is there a serious concern about the Legislature self-funding? Yes — Prop 4 permits the state itself to create a program by statute. That means legislators could vote to fund their own campaigns. That's a genuine conflict-of-interest concern. But it would require an appropriation and, for most parts, 2/3 vote to amend the section. Also they'd be accountable to voters.

Cost: LAO says state direct cost a few hundred thousand/year. Any program costs are opt-in by each government. So Prop 4 itself costs essentially nothing. This is a crucial point — the "blank check" framing is inaccurate as a matter of the measure's direct fiscal effect. The LAO, a nonpartisan fiscal authority, confirms: the measure creates no program and spends no money; only a few hundred thousand a year for FPPC guidance.

Now, weighing:

Arguments FOR a Yes vote:
1. It's permissive, not mandatory. Zero direct cost. It doesn't spend a single taxpayer dollar on campaigns by itself.
2. California is a national outlier — the only state with a blanket statutory ban (per Yes campaign; the LAO confirms the ban applies to most state/local offices).
3. The 1988 ban was enacted in a very different era (pre-Citizens United). Since Citizens United (2010), independent expenditures are unlimited and unmatchable by contribution limits. Public financing is one of the few remaining constitutional tools (Buckley v. Valeo explicitly endorsed public financing as furthering a significant government interest).
4. Empirical evidence: LA's 6:1 matching program produced candidates averaging ~6,600 contributions of ~$530 each vs. non-participants' ~560 contributions of ~$25,000 each (GAO). Seattle Democracy Vouchers: donors per race +350%, sub-$200 donations +270%, candidates +86%. NYC small-donor public financing helped elect the most diverse city council. SF Ethics Commission found increased uptake and third-party spending at near all-time lows.
5. Meaningful guardrails are included: no education/transportation/public-safety money; mandatory expenditure limits; small-donor qualifying (max $10 counted per donor); no legal defense fees or fines; no repayment of personal loans (ever, from any source — the Swalwell loophole); no incumbency or party discrimination.
6. It triples fines for illegal foreign campaign money — a genuine election-security improvement.
7. Endorsed by: Gov. Newsom, CA Democratic Party, League of Women Voters, Common Cause, Consumer Watchdog, CA Nurses Association, ACLU of Northern California, CA Labor Federation, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy boards, LA Times (Skelton), Bay Area Reporter, SPUR, and — notably — the SF Chronicle's own voter guide tool lists "Yes" (their editorial board said no, though).
8. Local control: any program would still need to be adopted locally — and in most cases would go to local voters as a charter amendment or tax measure. Voters retain the final say on spending.

Arguments FOR a No vote:
1. Design vagueness: no dollar amounts, no minimum meaningful spending caps, no required independent oversight body. The FPPC is explicitly exempted from administering/enforcing local programs, and local governments aren't required to create their own watchdog. SF Chronicle's point is well-taken — the Farrell case shows enforcement matters.
2. Evidence on whether public financing reduces big-money influence is mixed (GAO 2010 found no evidence of more candidates in AZ/ME; Oakland 2013 found no reduction in wealthy donor influence). Independent expenditures post-Citizens United swamp candidate-level funds — SF's 2024 record $8.8M in public funds vs. $19M in outside spending.
3. Cost: programs cost real money at a time of local budget stress. SF pays $8.8M per cycle. Oakland voters approved Democracy Dollars but the city hasn't funded it — showing either fiscal strain or poor follow-through.
4. Taxpayer compulsion: taxpayers fund speech they oppose (CalTax First Amendment objection). Counter: same is true of all public spending, and the Supreme Court has rejected compelled-speech challenges to public financing.
5. Voters have rejected repeal three times (2000: 34.7%, 2006: 25.7%, 2010: 42.7%) and current polling shows it losing (PPIC 42–53; Berkeley IGS 35–35 with 30% undecided; late Oct 41–35).
6. Legislature could self-fund — incumbents writing their own campaign subsidies.
7. Subdivision (f)'s spending-limit "trigger" resembles Arizona's scheme struck down in Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) — potential litigation risk. Mitigated by subdivision (i), which lets the Legislature amend (e), (f), and (h) by 2/3 vote.

Let me verify one more thing: the amendment standard. The californiatoday table says: "The definitions, the spending-limit formula and the FPPC clause can be amended by the Legislature under the Political Reform Act's usual standard, a two-thirds vote in each house... Every other part of the new section 85300, including the earmark exclusion and the ban on using public funds for fines and loan repayment, could be changed only with voters' approval."

Wait — the text says subdivision (i): "Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) of this section may be amended by statute pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 81012. The remaining subdivisions of this section may be amended only by a statute that complies with subdivision (b) of Section 81012."

Section 81012: (a) allows amendment by 2/3 of each house if it furthers the purposes of the act; (b) allows amendment by majority vote if approved by the voters... Let me check. Actually Gov Code 81012: "The provisions of this act may be amended by statute..." Hmm. Let me verify: Proposition 9 (1974) — the Political Reform Act — Article: "No amendment to this Act shall be effective unless approved by the voters, except that the Legislature may amend... by a two-thirds vote in each house if the amendment furthers the purposes of this Act." So (a) = 2/3 vote furthers purposes; (b) = voter approval. So subdivisions (e), (f), (h) can be fixed by 2/3 legislative vote; the rest needs voter approval. That's actually a well-designed feature — it locks in the taxpayer protections (earmark exclusion, no legal fees/fines/loan repayment, spending limits, neutrality) against simple-majority legislative dilution, while leaving technical definitions flexible.

Hmm, so actually this is a strength: the core safeguards can only be removed by the voters. Good.

Let me quickly verify 81012 to be accurate.

Also, let me check the LA Times editorial board's position on Prop 4 — the cityhallpass site said "We found no LA Times editorial board position." George Skelton personally said Yes. Let me confirm.

Let me also double-check the "Only state that bans public funding" claim and confirm there's no hidden mandate. And check the KQED voter guide for any additional analysis.

Let me do a couple more verification searches.

# Code Section
#### TITLE 9. POLITICAL REFORM [81000 - 91014]
##### CHAPTER 1. General [81000 - 81015]
###### 81012.
This title may be amended or repealed by the procedures set forth in this section.
If any portion of subdivision (a) is declared invalid, then subdivision (b) shall be the exclusive means of amending or repealing this title.
(a) This title may be amended to further its purposes by statute, passed in each house by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring and signed by the Governor, if at least 8 days before passage in each house, or at least 12 days before passage in each house if the previous form of the bill did not amend this title, the bill in its final form has been printed, distributed to the Members of the Legislature, and published on the internet.
(b) This title may be amended or repealed by a statute that becomes effective only when approved by the electors.

California Elections (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california)
Proposition 4
Should state and local governments have the option to provide public funding for election campaigns?
The measure would allow any state or local government to set up a public financing program for election campaigns. Candidates would need to meet certain eligibility criteria and agree to spending limits. The funds could not be used for legal defense costs, fines or repayment of personal loans. Proposition 4 would repeal a 1988 ban on using taxpayer dollars for election campaigns. Currently, only charter cities and counties can bypass that ban.
Yes Argument
Elections shouldn’t be determined by who has the greatest personal wealth or access to special interests. This measure would fight the influence of corporate money and super PACs by giving communities the opportunity to explore public financing programs that can help women, people of color and working-class candidates run competitive campaigns. It’s nonpartisan and prohibits public financing programs from favoring incumbents or political parties.
No Argument
Taxpayer dollars should be used for public services — like schools, roads and libraries — not political campaigns. At a time when cities and counties need more revenue for essential services, public financing opens the door to wasted taxpayer money on candidates who may never appear on the ballot. The measure is written too broadly, leaving each government to set its own eligibility criteria and spending limits, making the system vulnerable to abuse.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me do one final check: is there any concern about the measure's interaction with the county central committees? And let me verify the LA Times position. Also let me quickly check whether there is a "compelled speech" First Amendment concern that would invalidate the measure (CalTax raised it). Under Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Ass'n and other cases, government speech subsidies are generally not compelled speech by taxpayers. The Supreme Court has upheld public financing repeatedly (Buckley). So low legal risk to the core repeal.

Let me do one more check on the LA Times editorial board and one on whether any progressive/anti-money-in-politics group opposes.

Actually, I have enough. Let me consider one more important thing: the "60 candidates for governor" claim — under Prop 4, would every candidate get taxpayer money? No: candidates must meet "strict criteria" demonstrating broad-based support (e.g., small-dollar contributions/vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents). So the "thousands of candidates get taxpayer money" claim is overstated — qualifying thresholds would filter. LA's program requires 100+ contributions of $5+ and $12,857 in qualified contributions. SF requires 100 contributions of $10-$100 totaling $10,000 for supervisors. That's a real filter. The opponents' argument is somewhat misleading.

Also the "no limit on how much" claim — true that Prop 4 sets no dollar amounts, but it mandates expenditure limits, which is a cap on spending by participating candidates. And each program sets its own amounts, subject to local voters (charter amendments typically require voter approval; new taxes require voter approval).

One more consideration: Is there a risk that a future Legislature creates a self-funding program for state legislative races? Possible but: (a) it'd require appropriations in a tight budget, (b) it'd require 2/3 to amend the section (though creating a new fund is by statute — a simple majority appropriation... actually creating a dedicated fund by statute = majority vote; but appropriating money generally requires... a simple majority for the budget, 2/3 for taxes). Hmm, so a majority-vote statute could create a state program. But that's exactly what "local control/democratic accountability" means. And notably, the Democratic supermajority could have created a state program — they haven't proposed one. SB 42 was purely enabling.

Let me also weigh: What is the actual expected effect? The most likely outcomes: more cities/counties (especially in the Bay Area and LA County) adopt matching-fund programs. Costs would be borne by those localities' voters who choose them. Downside risk: some poorly designed programs with weak oversight. Upside: expanded candidate pools, more small donors, less reliance on megadonors.

Given:
- The measure itself spends nothing (LAO-confirmed).
- It's purely permissive and preserves local democratic choice.
- It contains real, voter-locked safeguards (education/transportation/public safety money protected; no legal fees/fines/personal loan repayment; mandatory expenditure limits; small-donor qualifying capped at $10/donor; no incumbency or party discrimination).
- Those safeguards can only be weakened by a 2/3 legislative vote or the voters themselves.
- It triples penalties for illegal foreign money in California elections — a genuine election-security upgrade.
- Post-Citizens United, public financing is one of the few constitutionally viable tools left to counter unlimited independent spending; California is the only state that forecloses it entirely.
- Strong evidence from matching-fund and voucher programs (LA, Seattle, NYC) that they dramatically broaden the donor base and candidate pool — precisely the "special interest" problem voters say they care about (85% in Pew).

Against:
- Weak/absent mandated independent oversight of local programs (the strongest substantive criticism).
- Mixed evidence on whether it actually reduces big-money influence; independent expenditures dwarf candidate funds.
- Real costs if adopted, at a time of local budget strain.
- Vagueness leaves design to the politicians who benefit.

Weighing: The criticisms are about how well future programs might be designed — but those programs are opt-in and, in most jurisdictions, would require a local vote (charter amendments/taxes). The "No" campaign's core claims ("blank check," "thousands of candidates," "less money for schools") are directly contradicted by the LAO's analysis and the measure's text (which explicitly wall-offs education, transportation, and public safety money). The measure has essentially zero fiscal impact, expands local democratic choice, removes a 38-year-old outlier ban that predates Citizens United, and adds an election-security penalty.

The oversight gap is real but is a design flaw in a permissive statute that future programs can and should cure — and it's not a reason to permanently lock every non-charter city and county in California out of an option available in all 49 other states.

I'll vote YES.

Let me do one final verification search on the LA Times and any progressive opposition to make sure I'm not missing something significant. Actually, let me do one quick check for any news about a lawsuit or a serious problem discovered late.
Let me do a final check for any late-breaking issues, litigation, or opposition I might have missed.

- It contains real, voter-locked safeguards (education/transportation/public safety money protected; no legal fees/fines/personal loan repayment; mandatory expenditure limits; small-donor qualifying capped at $10/donor; no incumbency or party discrimination).
- Those safeguards can only be weakened by a 2/3 legislative vote or the voters themselves.
- It triples penalties for illegal foreign money in California elections — a genuine election-security upgrade.
- Post-Citizens United, public financing is one of the few constitutionally viable tools left to counter unlimited independent spending; California is the only state that forecloses it entirely.
- Strong evidence from matching-fund and voucher programs (LA, Seattle, NYC) that they dramatically broaden the donor base and candidate pool — precisely the "special interest" problem voters say they care about (85% in Pew).

Against:
- Weak/absent mandated independent oversight of local programs (the strongest substantive criticism).
- Mixed evidence on whether it actually reduces big-money influence; independent expenditures dwarf candidate funds.
- Real costs if adopted, at a time of local budget strain.
- Vagueness leaves design to the politicians who benefit.

Weighing: The criticisms are about how well future programs might be designed — but those programs are opt-in and, in most jurisdictions, would require a local vote (charter amendments/taxes). The "No" campaign's core claims ("blank check," "thousands of candidates," "less money for schools") are directly contradicted by the LAO's analysis and the measure's text (which explicitly wall-offs education, transportation, and public safety money). The measure has essentially zero fiscal impact, expands local democratic choice, removes a 38-year-old outlier ban that predates Citizens United, and adds an election-security penalty.

The oversight gap is real but is a design flaw in a permissive statute that future programs can and should cure — and it's not a reason to permanently lock every non-charter city and county in California out of an option available in all 49 other states.

I'll vote YES.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me do one final check: is there any concern about the measure's interaction with the county central committees? And let me verify the LA Times position. Also let me quickly check whether there is a "compelled speech" First Amendment concern that would invalidate the measure (CalTax raised it). Under Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Ass'n and other cases, government speech subsidies are generally not compelled speech by taxpayers. The Supreme Court has upheld public financing repeatedly (Buckley). So low legal risk to the core repeal.

Let me do one more check on the LA Times editorial board and one on whether any progressive/anti-money-in-politics group opposes.

Actually, I have enough. Let me consider one more important thing: the "60 candidates for governor" claim — under Prop 4, would every candidate get taxpayer money? No: candidates must meet "strict criteria" demonstrating broad-based support (e.g., small-dollar contributions/vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents). So the "thousands of candidates get taxpayer money" claim is overstated — qualifying thresholds would filter. LA's program requires 100+ contributions of $5+ and $12,857 in qualified contributions. SF requires 100 contributions of $10-$100 totaling $10,000 for supervisors. That's a real filter. The opponents' argument is somewhat misleading.

Also the "no limit on how much" claim — true that Prop 4 sets no dollar amounts, but it mandates expenditure limits, which is a cap on spending by participating candidates. And each program sets its own amounts, subject to local voters (charter amendments typically require voter approval; new taxes require voter approval).

One more consideration: Is there a risk that a future Legislature creates a self-funding program for state legislative races? Possible but: (a) it'd require appropriations in a tight budget, (b) it'd require 2/3 to amend the section (though creating a new fund is by statute — a simple majority appropriation... actually creating a dedicated fund by statute = majority vote; but appropriating money generally requires... a simple majority for the budget, 2/3 for taxes). Hmm, so a majority-vote statute could create a state program. But that's exactly what "local control/democratic accountability" means. And notably, the Democratic supermajority could have created a state program — they haven't proposed one. SB 42 was purely enabling.

Let me also weigh: What is the actual expected effect? The most likely outcomes: more cities/counties (especially in the Bay Area and LA County) adopt matching-fund programs. Costs would be borne by those localities' voters who choose them. Downside risk: some poorly designed programs with weak oversight. Upside: expanded candidate pools, more small donors, less reliance on megadonors.

Given:
- The measure itself spends nothing (LAO-confirmed).
- It's purely permissive and preserves local democratic choice.
- It contains real, voter-locked safeguards (education/transportation/public safety money protected; no legal fees/fines/personal loan repayment; mandatory expenditure limits; small-donor qualifying capped at $10/donor; no incumbency or party discrimination).
- Those safeguards can only be weakened by a 2/3 legislative vote or the voters themselves.
- It triples penalties for illegal foreign money in California elections — a genuine election-security upgrade.
- Post-Citizens United, public financing is one of the few constitutionally viable tools left to counter unlimited independent spending; California is the only state that forecloses it entirely.
- Strong evidence from matching-fund and voucher programs (LA, Seattle, NYC) that they dramatically broaden the donor base and candidate pool — precisely the "special interest" problem voters say they care about (85% in Pew).

Against:
- Weak/absent mandated independent oversight of local programs (the strongest substantive criticism).
- Mixed evidence on whether it actually reduces big-money influence; independent expenditures dwarf candidate funds.
- Real costs if adopted, at a time of local budget strain.
- Vagueness leaves design to the politicians who benefit.

Weighing: The criticisms are about how well future programs might be designed — but those programs are opt-in and, in most jurisdictions, would require a local vote (charter amendments/taxes). The "No" campaign's core claims ("blank check," "thousands of candidates," "less money for schools") are directly contradicted by the LAO's analysis and the measure's text (which explicitly wall-offs education, transportation, and public safety money). The measure has essentially zero fiscal impact, expands local democratic choice, removes a 38-year-old outlier ban that predates Citizens United, and adds an election-security penalty.

The oversight gap is real but is a design flaw in a permissive statute that future programs can and should cure — and it's not a reason to permanently lock every non-charter city and county in California out of an option available in all 49 other states.

I'll vote YES.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I now have a very thorough picture. Let me synthesize and decide.

Key facts established:
1. **What it is**: Prop 4 (SB 42, Umberg, Ch. 245 of 2025), the California Fair Elections Act of 2026. Repeals Government Code §85300's blanket ban on public campaign financing (from Prop 73, 1988) and replaces it with conditional permission. Also triples fines for illegal foreign campaign money (§85320).

2. **Fiscal impact**: LAO — no program created, no money spent. State cost: "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for FPPC guidance (FPPC asked for ~$205K first year, $198K/yr after). Less than 0.1% of the General Fund. Local costs only if a government opts in.

3. **Guardrails in the text**:
   - Money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used.
   - Participating candidates must accept expenditure limits.
   - Must demonstrate broad-based support via small-dollar contributions/vouchers; max countable contribution $10.
   - No public funds for legal defense fees or fines.
   - No repayment of personal campaign loans from public funds — ever, from any source, even after the campaign ends.
   - Programs may not discriminate by party or incumbency; funds available to all qualified candidates for the same office.
   - Amendment protection: subdivisions (e), (f), (h) amendable by 2/3 legislature; ALL OTHER subdivisions (including the earmark protection, expenditure limits, legal-fee/loan bans, neutrality) require voter approval under §81012(b). So the core taxpayer protections are locked in against simple-majority legislative dilution.

4. **Context**: California is the only state with a blanket statutory ban (Johnson v. Bradley (1992) carved out charter cities only). 15 states + DC and ~26 localities have programs. The ban predates Citizens United (2010) by 22 years — it was written for a world where contribution limits could actually constrain campaign money. Now unlimited independent expenditures are the dominant force; Buckley v. Valeo affirmed public financing "furthers a significant governmental interest."

5. **Evidence**: Mixed but with strong positives on the specific outcomes that matter:
   - LA 2022 mayoral: publicly financed candidates averaged ~6,600 contributions of ~$530; non-participants ~560 contributions of ~$25,000 (GAO).
   - Seattle Democracy Vouchers: donors per race +350%, sub-$200 donations +270%, candidates +86%; voucher users ~12x more likely to vote; low-income residents and people of color more likely to use vouchers.
   - Berkeley after 2018: non-resident contributions fell from 33% to 10%.
   - NYC small-donor matching helped elect the most diverse city council.
   - GAO (2025): publicly financed candidates won/advanced in ≥50% of contests in 4 of 5 studied jurisdictions.
   - Counter-evidence: GAO 2010 found no increase in candidates in AZ/ME; Oakland 2013 found no reduction in wealthy-donor influence; a 2017 peer-reviewed study found LA's program design "substantially less effective" than NYC's; little evidence public financing curbs overall private-donor influence.
   
   Honest read: design matters enormously. Programs with high match rates + low qualifying thresholds + vouchers work; poorly designed ones don't.

6. **Weaknesses of Prop 4** (the strongest genuine criticisms):
   - Explicitly exempts FPPC from administering/enforcing local programs, and does NOT require local governments to create an independent oversight body. The SF Chronicle's Mark Farrell example is a fair illustration of why enforcement matters.
   - No mandated design standards (match rates, qualifying thresholds, minimum meaningful spending caps), so a jurisdiction could adopt an ineffective or self-serving program.
   - Legislature could theoretically create a state program funding its own campaigns.
   - Subdivision (f)'s spending-limit escalation formula resembles Arizona's matching-funds trigger struck down in Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) — litigation risk. (Mitigated: (f) is amendable by 2/3 legislature.)

7. **Weaknesses of the "No" case**:

**Yes.**

---

**What it actually is** (note: this is the Nov 3, **2026** ballot — Prop 4 here is SB 42/Ch. 245 of 2025, the "California Fair Elections Act," not the 2024 climate bond). It repeals the 1988 Prop 73 blanket ban on public campaign financing (Gov. Code §85300) and replaces it with conditional permission. It creates no program and appropriates nothing. It also triples fines for illegal foreign campaign money.

**Why yes:**

- **It costs essentially nothing.** The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst confirms no program is created and no campaign money is spent; state cost is "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for FPPC guidance — under 0.1% of the General Fund. Local costs arise only if a government opts in, and in practice via a charter amendment or tax vote, so local voters still get final say on any real spending.
- **The "blank check / less money for schools" attack is contradicted by the text and the LAO.** Education, transportation, and public-safety money is explicitly walled off. Expenditure limits are *mandatory*. Qualifying must be small-dollar (no contribution over $10 can be required to count). Public funds can never pay legal defense fees, fines, or repay a candidate's personal loan — ever, from any source.
- **The safeguards are unusually well-locked.** Under Gov. Code §81012(b), those protections can be stripped only by the voters, not by a simple legislative majority. Only the technical definitions/escalation formula/FPPC clause are 2/3-amendable.
- **California is the sole state with a blanket ban** — an artifact of 1988, 22 years pre-*Citizens United*. With unlimited independent spending now dominant, small-donor public financing is one of the few constitutionally viable tools left (*Buckley*: it "furthers a significant governmental interest"). $1B+ spent on state candidate races since 2020; the most expensive governor's race in U.S. history.
- **The best-designed programs show real results.** LA 2022: publicly financed candidates averaged ~6,600 contributions of ~$530 vs. ~560 of ~$25,000 for non-participants (GAO). Seattle vouchers: candidates +86%, donors per race +350%, voucher users far likelier to vote. Berkeley: non-resident money fell 33%→10%. GAO found publicly financed candidates won/advanced in ≥50% of contests in 4 of 5 jurisdictions studied.
- **Voting no is the irreversible choice.** A bad local program can be repealed locally. A "no" keeps a permanent statewide prohibition that only another ballot measure can lift — and guarantees California never learns from its own experiments.

**The strongest honest objection** (SF Chronicle): Prop 4 exempts the FPPC from enforcing local programs and doesn't require an independent local watchdog, and it sets no design standards — the Mark Farrell SF case shows enforcement matters. That's a real flaw. But it's a fixable design gap in an *opt-in* statute, not a reason to permanently exclude every non-charter city, all 58 counties, all districts and the state from an option available in all 49 other states.

Context worth knowing: it polls behind (PPIC 42–53; Berkeley IGS 35–35, later 41–35) and similar repeals failed in 2000, 2006 and 2010. The No side raised $0 with no registered committee; Yes raised ~$992K (nurses' union, Movement Voter PAC, labor federation, ACLU NorCal). Backed by Newsom, League of Women Voters, Common Cause, Consumer Watchdog, the McClatchy California boards and SPUR; opposed by CalTax, Howard Jarvis, Reform California, the Chronicle, the Union-Tribune and SCNG papers.

   - LA 2022 mayoral: publicly financed candidates averaged ~6,600 contributions of ~$530; non-participants ~560 contributions of ~$25,000 (GAO).
   - Seattle Democracy Vouchers: donors per race +350%, sub-$200 donations +270%, candidates +86%; voucher users ~12x more likely to vote; low-income residents and people of color more likely to use vouchers.
   - Berkeley after 2018: non-resident contributions fell from 33% to 10%.
   - NYC small-donor matching helped elect the most diverse city council.
   - GAO (2025): publicly financed candidates won/advanced in ≥50% of contests in 4 of 5 studied jurisdictions.
   - Counter-evidence: GAO 2010 found no increase in candidates in AZ/ME; Oakland 2013 found no reduction in wealthy-donor influence; a 2017 peer-reviewed study found LA's program design "substantially less effective" than NYC's; little evidence public financing curbs overall private-donor influence.

6. **Weaknesses of Prop 4** (the strongest genuine criticisms):
   - Explicitly exempts FPPC from administering/enforcing local programs, and does NOT require local governments to create an independent oversight body. The SF Chronicle's Mark Farrell example is a fair illustration of why enforcement matters.
   - No mandated design standards (match rates, qualifying thresholds, minimum meaningful spending caps), so a jurisdiction could adopt an ineffective or self-serving program.
   - Legislature could theoretically create a state program funding its own campaigns.
   - Subdivision (f)'s spending-limit escalation formula resembles Arizona's matching-funds trigger struck down in Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) — litigation risk. (Mitigated: (f) is amendable by 2/3 legislature.)

7. **Weaknesses of the "No" case**:
   - "Blank check," "less money for schools, less money for public safety" — directly contradicted by the measure's text, which wall-offs education, transportation, and public safety money, and by the LAO, which says no program is created and no money is spent.
   - "Thousands of candidates get taxpayer money" — contradicted by the mandatory "strict criteria" showing broad-based support (real programs require 100+ resident small-dollar contributions, e.g., LA and SF).

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

# Climate Bond (Proposition 4)
### Climate Bond (Proposition 4)
Proposition 4, Safe Drinking Water, Wildfire Prevention, Drought Preparedness, and Clean Air Bond Act of 2024, also known as the Climate Bond, authorized $10 billion in bonds to finance projects addressing California’s climate change, water resiliency, natural resources, wildfires, and other environmental projects.
From the $10 billion, $300 million was designated for agriculture, of that, $255 million was allocated for climate smart agriculture and resiliency programs at the California Department of Food and Agriculture.
### CDFA Climate Bond Programs
#### Regional Farm Equipment Sharing Program ($15 million)
In November 2024, California voters approved Proposition 4, also known as the Climate Bond.
This historic $10 billion investment helps safeguard our communities, natural resources, and future in the face of climate change.
...
How Does the Climate Bond Advance California’s Goals
The Climate Bond advances the state’s overarching goals of protecting Californians from climate impacts and achieving carbon neutrality through nature-based solutions.
It does this by helping local communities adapt by restoring and conserving natural landscapes that reduce extreme heat and wildfire risk, improve drought and flood resilience, and support clean air and water.
It also invests in essential infrastructure and ensures access to clean drinking water, healthy local food, and safe, welcoming outdoor spaces.

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
The Political Reform Act. Many people, groups, and businesses spend money to support or oppose candidates for public office and ballot measures. California's Political Reform Act sets rules for how money can be used in politics and requires public reporting of political spending. These rules apply to state and local candidates, ballot measures, and other public officials, but not to federal candidates or officials. (Federal law establishes campaign finance and reporting requirements for federal offices.) The Political Reform Act has been updated by voters over the years.
Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns. The Political Reform Act bans the use of public funds for political candidates' campaigns. This ban applies to most elected offices at the state level and local level. (This ban does not apply to city office elections in certain charter cities. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley are current examples of charter cities that provide public funds to certain campaigns.)
Entities That Oversee Campaign Finance Laws. California's campaign finance laws are administered by the Fair Political Practices Commission and the California Secretary of State. State law requires people and groups to report how much money they give, receive, and spend on political campaigns. This information is available to the public on the Secretary of State's website. The Fair Political Practices Commission enforces and interprets the Political Reform Act. The Fair Political Practices Commission reviews the finance reports and can fine candidates and donors who break the law. The Fair Political Practices Commission issues guidance based on its interpretation of the Political Reform Act.
PROPOSAL
Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates' Campaigns. Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates' campaigns. Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers. Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program. For example, money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns. Candidates can only receive public funds if they show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits and other program rules. Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate's personal campaign loan. State and local governments can design and implement their own programs within the broad rules set by Proposition 4.
Fair Political Practices Commission Would Issue Guidance on Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 specifies that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not required to administer or enforce local public campaign finance programs. Rather, state and local government officials could ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on how to create public campaign finance programs consistent with Proposition 4.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Costs of Possible Public Campaign Finance Programs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance program. However, it allows state and local governments to create such programs in the future. The cost of these programs could be significant for governments that choose to create them. The total cost would depend on which governments created such programs and how those programs were designed.
Minor State Costs to Support State and Local Governments Considering Public Campaign Finance Programs. If voters approve Proposition 4, state and local government officials likely would ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on creating public campaign finance programs under the Political Reform Act. This likely would require the Fair Political Practices Commission to hire more legal staff to help answer these questions. As a result, state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars each year. This amount is much less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
YES ON PROPOSITION 4, THE CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT: ELECTIONS SHOULD BE WON, NOT BOUGHT
The amount of money in California elections is outrageous; it's distorting our democracy. Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone. This massive spending gives special interests greater access and influence while drowning out the voices of ordinary Californians.
PROP. 4 HELPS QUALIFIED CANDIDATES COMPETE
Running for office today often requires either personal wealth or access to wealthy donors. Deep pockets have become an unofficial requirement to run for office, leaving too many qualified candidates behind.
PROP. 4 CHANGES THE WAY WE FINANCE ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
Programs like small-dollar donation matching help candidates compete without relying on wealthy donors. However, most California communities are banned from using these tools, allowing the influence of big money to grow.
Proposition 4 lifts that ban, giving voters and local governments the option to adopt public financing with strict safeguards so qualified candidates-regardless of their income-can compete against candidates who are backed by wealthy interests.
PROP. 4 BUILDS ON A PROVEN MODEL
We know this reform works because it's working in other states. Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems. They are new people with good ideas from all walks of life. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their mind and work for the people, not the special interests.
PROP. 4 GIVES LOCAL COMMUNITIES A CHOICE
Proposition 4 does not create a public financing program. It simply gives local governments the option to adopt one if they choose.
If a community does, the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year-a small investment to help counter the billions spent influencing California's elections.
PROP. 4 PROTECTS TAXPAYERS
Taxpayer Safeguards:
Requires candidates to meet strict eligibility criteria and abide by spending limits to qualify for public funds.
Prohibits public funding from favoring incumbents or discriminating based on political party.
Prohibits the use of public funds for legal defense or fines.
PROP. 4 CRACKS DOWN ON ILLEGAL FOREIGN MONEY
Proposition 4 triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions and expenditures, strengthening penalties for those who attempt to interfere in California's elections.
PROP. 4 IS SUPPORTED BY LEADERS ACROSS CALIFORNIA
Proposition 4 is backed by a broad coalition including League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy Services, Social Security Works, California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California National Organization for Women, Californians for Disability Rights, Consumer Watchdog, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In, Voters Right to Know, and many others.
PROP. 4 GIVES CALIFORNIANS THE OPPORTUNITY TO RECLAIM THEIR ELECTIONS and ensure they reflect the values of the people, not just the wealthiest donors.
YES ON 4-Restore power to voters, not wealthy donors
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Tom Umberg , California State Senator
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
Here is what the politicians supporting Proposition 4 do not tell you:
Proposition 4 REPEALS the voter-approved law that PROHIBITS candidates from using taxpayer money to run for office.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money. In the election last June, more than 60 candidates ran for Governor. Proposition 4 would allow thousands of candidates to get taxpayer money!
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get. Proposition 4 opens the door to taxpayer-funded campaigns but provides no limits on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get and NO LIMIT on spending. It will lead to more negative ads, more junk mail, and more annoying text messages.
Proposition 4 does NOT PROHIBIT SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY in campaigns. Proposition 4 ALLOWS candidates to get taxpayer money AND to get special interest money! Where exactly is the money going to come from to fund thousands of political campaigns? Proposition 4 does not say. But you know the answer. It is coming from YOU, the taxpayers! Less money for schools, less money for public safety, less money for healthcare. More money for politicians.
Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. It is based on false promises and failed solutions.
Proposition 4 does NOT protect taxpayers. That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by California's leading taxpayer organizations.
Proposition 4 does NOT provide for “fair elections.” That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by former Commissioners of the Fair Political Practices Commission.
Vote NO ON PROPOSITION 4.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 4
Why did Sacramento politicians put Proposition 4 on the ballot? They want access to YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY to fund THEIR OWN CAMPAIGNS.
Proposition 4 repeals a voter approved law that PROHIBITS these politicians from using public taxpayer funds for their own campaigns. That's right, Proposition 4 allows politicians to use your taxpayer money to fund their campaigns.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get! Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. There isn't even a limit on how much they can spend on their campaigns! More negative ads. More junk mail. More annoying text messages. More, more, more.
Proposition 4 is so poorly written, it could allow every state or local “candidate” to get public funding. They don't even have to actually qualify for the ballot to get taxpayer money. Proposition 4 allows for public funding of thousands of state and local candidates. It even allows for public financing of candidates for county political party committees.
In just the last primary election, there were more than 60 candidates for Governor. Do you want YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY going to support more of their negative campaign ads and junk mail?
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can receive. It says it requires “strict criteria” to receive taxpayer funds but provides NO DETAILS on what the criteria are! Read the fine print:
“‘Strict criteria' means the requirement set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds.”
But there is no current statute, ordinance or charter setting any criteria. Guess who will be setting the criteria? The same politicians who want to get your taxpayer money!
Some good government groups support public financing of campaigns because they want to get special interest money out of politics. BUT PROPOSITION 4 DOES NOT GET RID OF SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY! Under Proposition 4, candidates can raise money from special interests AND get public funding too.
Proposition 4 is the worst kind of public financing scheme. It provides no specifics. It leaves all the details to be worked out by the same politicians who want to get access to public funds.
It is a blank check. But worse than that, Proposition 4 allows special-interest funding of political campaigns.
Please join California's leading taxpayer protection organizations, including the California Taxpayers Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California, United Latinos Action, as well as former members of California's Fair Political Practices Commission, who all oppose Proposition 4.
PLEASE VOTE NO ON THE POLITICIANS' BLANK CHECK PROPOSITION. VOTE NO ON PROP. 4.
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
Colleen McAndrews , Former Commissioner
Fair Political Practices Commission
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 4
DON'T BE MISLED BY SPECIAL INTERESTS WHO WANT TO KEEP BUYING ELECTIONS
California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns. Communities in all 49 other states have the right to adopt public financing to allow qualified candidates to compete against wealthy donors. California doesn't. Prop. 4 simply removes that ban and gives local voters the same choice everyone else has, while instituting strict taxpayer safeguards.
PROP. 4 GIVES POWER BACK TO LOCAL COMMUNITIES AND EMPOWERS VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Prop. 4 doesn't spend a single taxpayer dollar or institute public financing anywhere. It simply removes the ban to give every city, county, and the state the right to adopt public funding if local voters want it. The details are appropriately left to each community. But any system MUST require candidates to abide by spending limits and demonstrate broad-based support in their district to qualify.
PROP. 4 MAKES ELECTED OFFICIALS ACCOUNTABLE TO VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Corporate special interests oppose Prop. 4 because public financing allows candidates to run and win without relying on them-threatening their grip on California elections.
Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected across the country using public financing, for a tiny cost. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their minds and work for the people, not special interests.
DON'T BE FOOLED BY CORPORATE SPECIAL INTERESTS HIDING BEHIND NICE-SOUNDING NAMES.
VOTE YES ON 4 to let local voters and communities reclaim their elections so they're won, not bought.
Carmen Balber , Executive Director
Consumer Watchdog

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. This act shall be known, and may be
cited, as the California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
SEC. 2. The Legislature finds and declares all of the
following:
(a) All citizens should be able to make their voices
heard in the political process and hold their elected
officials accountable.
4 (b) Elections for local or state elective office should be
fair, open, and competitive.
(c) The increasing costs of political campaigns can
force candidates to rely on large contributions from
wealthy donors and special interests, which can give
those wealthy donors and special interests
disproportionate influence over governmental
decisions.
(d) Such disproportionate influence can undermine
the public’s trust that public officials are performing
their duties in an impartial manner and that government
is serving the needs and responding to the wishes of all
citizens equally, without regard to their wealth.
(e) Special interests contribute more to incumbents
than challengers because they seek access to elected
officials, and such contributions account for a large
portion of the financial incumbency advantage, as
confirmed by studies such as those published in the
Journal of Politics in 2014 and Political Research
Quarterly in 2016.
(f) Citizen-funded election programs, in which
qualified candidates can receive public funds for the
purpose of communicating with voters rather than
relying exclusively on private donors, are currently
operative in five charter cities in California, as well as
numerous other local and state jurisdictions.
(g) Citizen-funded election programs encourage
competition by reducing the financial advantages of
incumbency and making it possible for citizens from all
walks of life, not only those with connections to wealthy
donors or special interests, to run for office, as
confirmed by studies such as those published in State
Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2008, and by the
Campaign Finance Institute in 2015, the National
Institute on Money in State Politics in 2016, and the
State Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2022.
(h) By reducing reliance on wealthy donors and special
interests, citizen-funded election programs inhibit
improper practices, protect against corruption or the
appearance of corruption, and protect the political
integrity of our governmental institutions.
(i) In Johnson v. Bradley (1992) 4 Cal.4th 389, the
California Supreme Court highlighted the Court of
Appeal’s observation that “it seems obvious that public
money reduces rather than increases the fund raising
pressures on public office seekers and thereby reduces
the undue influence of special interest groups.”

(j) In Buckley v. Valeo (1976) 424 U.S. 1, the United
States Supreme Court recognized that “public
financing as a means of eliminating the improper
influence of large private contributions furthers a
significant governmental interest.”
(k) In Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) 564
U.S. 721, the United States Supreme Court
acknowledged that public financing of elections “can
further ‘significant governmental interest[s]’ such as
the state interest in preventing corruption,” quoting
Buckley v. Valeo.
(l) In Buckley v. Valeo, the United States Supreme
Court further noted that citizen-funded elections
programs “facilitate and enlarge public discussion and
participation in the electoral process, goals vital to a
self-governing people.”
(m) The absolute prohibition on public campaign
financing allows special interests to gain
disproportionate influence and unfairly favors
incumbents. An exception should be created to permit
citizen-funded election programs so that elections may
be conducted more fairly.

# Proposition 4
Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns.
Legislative Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates’ Campaigns.*** Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates’ campaigns.
Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish.
Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
***Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs.*** Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers.
Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program.
For example, money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns.
Candidates can only receive public funds if they show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits and other program rules.
Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan.

In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.

“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”
ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026)
2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/)
Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know
Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

Prop
4
CA
Prop
4
|
Statute
Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
Repeals the ban on public financing of campaigns and allows state or local governments to establish programs that provide candidates with public funding under preestablished spending limits and eligibility requirements.
SPUR's Recommendation
California campaigns are expensive and donor-dependent. Public financing brings in more small-dollar donors, lowers barriers for first-time and under-resourced candidates, and increases candidate diversity and voter engagement. These benefits align with SPUR’s view that equitable representation requires campaign finance reform. Financing programs would add costs and create administrative burden, but because governments would opt in to Prop. 4, they would retain flexibility over whether and how to implement it. SPUR supports clearing this state-level barrier and letting cities, counties, and the state decide for themselves.
Vote YES
What Prop. 4 Would Do
Proposition 4 would give state and local jurisdictions the option of creating a public financing program for candidates running for office. If state and local governments opt in, they would have to develop spending limits and criteria for candidates to qualify for public funds. Candidates would be barred from using public finance dollars for legal defense fees, fines, or to repay personal loans to a campaign. The source of funding, such as a city’s General Fund or a property tax, is left to local governments, but the funds cannot come from money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
The Backstory
California has one main law governing campaign finance. In 1974, Proposition 9 created the Political Reform Act. This act regulates campaign finance disclosure, contributions, expenditures, lobbying practices, and government conflicts of interest and ethics. It has been amended more than 200 times. In 1988, Proposition 73 banned public campaign funding on the grounds that too much money was being spent on political campaigns and that public funds should be directed to other priorities.
Since then, several ballot measures have attempted to reshape the state’s public financing landscape with varying success. Proposition 34, passed in 2000, imposed contribution, transfer, and voluntary spending limits for candidates listed in the ballot pamphlet that remain largely in effect today. In 2016, the Legislature passed a measure that would have lifted the state’s ban on public financing, but the courts ruled that it needed to go to the voters. The legislature addressed this issue in 2025, resulting in Prop. 4 on the 2026 ballot.
Wealthy donors and corporate-funded political ads often dominate elections in California, sidelining everyday voters and eroding public trust in government. Lobbying groups spent more than $500 million to influence the state government in 2024, the most ever. 1 Prop. 4 does not set a limit on this activity but aims to help level the playing field by providing public funding to candidates who do not have access to support from wealthy individuals or corporations.
Campaigns have become increasingly expensive to run at all levels. At the state level, according to the organization Common Cause, it costs roughly $1 million to run and win a California Assembly seat and $1.7 million to run and win a State Senate seat. 2 As a result, megadonors and outside interests routinely foot the bill and, in the process, discourage those without wealthy networks from running.
Current state law permits public campaign financing only in charter cities, not at the state level or in non-charter cities. Of California's 121 charter cities, 6 have public financing programs: Berkeley, Long Beach, Los Angeles, Oakland, Richmond, and San Francisco. Nationally, 20 other cities and counties and 14 states have public campaign financing. Public financing programs vary from grants and vouchers to matching programs. Los Angeles and San Francisco have a 6:1 matching fund — every $1 donated by a resident is matched by $6 from the city — with a cap depending on the office a candidate is running for. Seattle and Oakland offer Democracy Dollars, whereby every resident over 18 receives four $25 vouchers to donate to their preferred local candidate(s).

Evidence suggests public campaign financing can lead to more small-dollar donors, greater donor diversity, and a broader range of people running for office. A 2022 University of Washington study found that in the two election cycles since Seattle implemented its program, the number of donors per race increased by 350%. Donations of less than $200 increased by 270%, and the number of candidates rose by 86% . A separate analysis also found that some residents were almost 12 times more likely to vote if they participated in the program, and low-income Seattleites and people of color were more likely to use their vouchers than they were to give a cash donation. 4
The Government Accountability Office's review of five programs (Arizona, Los Angeles, Minnesota, Montgomery County, Maryland, and Seattle) found that publicly financed candidates performed better than candidates who did not opt in. A participating candidate won or advanced in at least 50% of all contests in four of the five locations — reaching 85% to 95% in some Minnesota and Los Angeles elections. In matching-fund and voucher programs, candidates consistently received far more, but smaller, contributions; for example, in Los Angeles's 2022 mayoral race, publicly financed candidates averaged around 6,600 contributions of about $530 each, while non-participants averaged approximately 560 contributions of almost $25,000 each.
Prop. 4 was placed on the ballot legislatively through Senate Bill 42 (2025) and requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Wealthy, often demographically narrow donor networks currently dominate California campaign funding, disproportionately affecting people by race, income, and geography. Oakland’s 2023 campaign finance measure (Measure W) was proposed to address this disparity. Research found that campaign contributions gave disproportionate power to donors outside Oakland and in the city's wealthier, whiter neighborhoods. 5 That disproportionate power muted the political voice of lower-income residents and communities of color in their own local elections.
Public financing can counter such impacts. In Seattle, low-income residents and people of color were more likely to use Democracy Dollars than to make a cash donation, meaning the model activates participation among populations least engaged by traditional, wealth-dependent giving. Voucher users were also substantially more likely to vote. By lowering the fundraising bar, public financing also opens pathways for candidates without wealthy networks (often candidates of color, women, and working-class candidates) to run competitively, diversifying who’s on the ballot, not just who funds them. Prop 4 could encourage more candidates to run for office and help the candidate pools better reflect local racial, gender, and socioeconomic diversity. 6
Because Prop. 4 is optional for cities, these equity gains depend on which jurisdictions adopt and properly fund programs (as the research on Oakland’s still-unfunded Measure W shows). But removing the state-level barrier allows every California city and county to build systems that broaden who can run and whose voices matter locally.
Pros
Prop. 4 could encourage more candidates to run for office who reflect California’s racial, gender, and socioeconomic diversity by lowering the barrier to entry for candidates without wealthy networks, name recognition, or fundraising experience.
The measure would foster more small donors and reduce reliance on big money.
Public campaign financing can increase voter engagement and turnout when using vouchers.
The measure would allow local flexibility and would be optional, rather than a mandate, reducing the risk of a one-size-fits-all system.
Cons
Evidence on whether public campaign financing can reduce big-money influence in elections is mixed. Prop. 4 would not limit campaign financing through independent expenditures and political action committees, which have had outsized influence on elections since the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision.
Prop. 4 would present a cost to taxpayers. Public financing requires ongoing public money through General Fund appropriations, dedicated taxes, or fees.
The measure would entail administrative burden and complexity. Campaign financing programs require qualification review, spending-limit enforcement, audits, fraud detection, and other processes.

The influence of money on political races has gotten out of control, but allowing candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes is not the answer.
We recommend voting “no” on Proposition 4. Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.

Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/11/whos-donating-to-the-billionaire-backed-group-has-raised-almost-300-million-to-fight-the-wealth-tax/) showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.
