Endorsement: California hasn’t even bothered to study its existing public financing programs. No on Prop 4
Proposition 4 would overturn California’s ban on public financing of campaigns but does not include key guardrails.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
There’s no excuse for Prop 4’s backers’ failure to do this homework, given that voters rejected efforts to lift California’s ban on public campaign financing in 2000 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html), 2006 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2006/89_11_2006.htm) and 2010 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2010/15_06_2010.aspx).
We encourage you to vote no again.

Good. This is a substantive legal concern. Prop 4's subdivision (f) allows increased expenditure limits based on "net supportive funds" of other candidates and independent expenditures — that's essentially a trigger mechanism similar to Arizona's, which was struck down in Bennett. However, subdivision (i) allows the Legislature to amend subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) by simple majority statute, so this is fixable.

But there's a more important point: even if (f) is struck down, the rest of the measure (lifting the ban) would remain. And the LAO analysis doesn't flag constitutional concerns.

Now let me look at:
1. Who funded Yes on 4 vs No on 4 (money behind the measure).
2. The San Diego Union-Tribune's editorial (the strongest "no" case).
3. Sacramento Bee's yes case.
4. Also, does the measure have any provision that might allow state legislators to create their own public financing? Yes — "state or a local governmental entity establishes a dedicated fund for this purpose by statute." So the Legislature could self-fund. That's a legitimate concern (conflict of interest). Though they'd need a 2/3 vote? Actually, creating a dedicated fund by statute — appropriations require majority, but a tax increase requires 2/3. Also, under Prop 4, amending remaining subdivisions requires compliance with 81012(b) = 2/3 vote.

5. Important: What about the "county political party committees" claim? The opponents claim Prop 4 allows public financing of candidates for county central committees. Let me check — Section 85300 applies to "public officer" and "candidate" for "elective office." County central committee members are elected partisan party positions — arguably "elective office." That's a real if minor drafting sloppiness.

Let me now look at money, and the SDUT editorial and Sacramento Bee editorial. Also let me check the Yes campaign's funders and whether it's dominated by particular interests.

Also check whether there is a fiscal estimate for local costs (Scott Alexander said ~$75 million in extra local taxes).

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

2026 California Prop 4 guide: "Public financing" measure would let state and local governments give candidates public money for their campaigns
Proposition 4 repeals the 1988 ban that keeps the state, counties and most cities from funding campaigns. It creates no program itself; any government that wants one would set the amounts, under rules on spending limits, small-donor support and money for schools, roads and public safety.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 18, 2026

California's Proposition 4 is asking voters whether the state and local governments may fund candidates' campaigns with public money.
Proposition 4 would repeal the California law that bars the state, counties and most cities from giving candidates public money for their campaigns, a ban voters approved in 1988.
It would not create a public financing program or spend money on any campaign. It would let the state and local governments build their own programs, under conditions written into the measure: candidates who take public funds must accept spending limits and show broad support in their district, typically through small donations, and no money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety can be used. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the state's direct cost at "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions, and says the cost of any program a government chooses to create "could be significant." The measure also raises the maximum fine for illegal campaign contributions from foreign sources.
California Proposition 4 is the fourth statewide attempt to lift the 1988 public campaign financing ban, after measures in 2000, 2006 and 2010 drew between 25.7% and 42.7% yes. Prop 4, the California Fair Elections Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/) placed on the ballot by SB 42, which Senator Tom Umberg wrote and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on October 2, 2025. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and one of three that change how California runs elections, alongside Proposition 5 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/california-proposition-5-2026/)'s recall changes and Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/)'s voter ID rules. California voters have turned down three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban, in 2000, 2006 and 2010, each of which also created a program; this is the first to ask only whether the ban should go. PPIC's September survey found 42% yes and 53% no, and UC Berkeley's found 35% on each side. Almost no money has been raised on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, the 1988 ban and the court fight over an earlier attempt to lift it, the cities that already fund campaigns, the cost, the arguments and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 4 replaces California's ban on public campaign funds with conditions for any future program:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf) rewrites Government Code section 85300, the one-sentence ban in the Political Reform Act. Today that section says a public officer "shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office." Prop 4 keeps the prohibition only for funds "earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety," which opens every other public source to a program a government chooses to create by statute, ordinance or charter.
It then sets the ground rules. Candidates "shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds." The measure defines strict criteria as requirements that make candidates "demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents." A program that counts small donors cannot require any donor to give more than $10 to be counted, and it cannot require candidates to collect signatures or reach a total dollar amount above $10 per contributor. Programs may not "discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent."
Three uses of the money are banned outright. Public funds cannot pay legal defense fees or fines, and no candidate can use them to repay a personal loan to their own campaign. A candidate who takes public funds also cannot repay such a loan from any source once the campaign ends.
The measure sets no dollar amounts. It does not say how much a candidate can receive, what a match would be or how high a spending limit must be; those are left to each statute, ordinance or charter. It does cap one thing: a program may raise a participating candidate's spending limit when opponents or outside groups outspend them, but only up to a formula in the text, the highest "net supportive funds" of any other candidate in the race plus outside spending against the participating candidate, minus outside spending for them.

section 85300. The state and any local government, by statute, ordinance or charter
Money that can be used None outside charter cities Any public funds except money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety
How candidates qualify Not applicable "Strict criteria" showing broad-based support in the district, such as small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a set number of voting-age residents. No signature requirement, and no contribution larger than $10 can be required for a donor to count.
Spending limits Not applicable Participating candidates must accept spending limits set by each program. A program may raise a candidate's limit when opponents or outside groups outspend them, up to a formula in the measure.
Neutrality Not applicable Programs may not discriminate by party or between incumbents and challengers
Barred uses of public money Not applicable Legal defense fees, fines and repaying a candidate's personal loan to the campaign. A publicly funded candidate may never repay such a loan from any source after the campaign ends.
Oversight FPPC enforces the ban FPPC answers questions but is not responsible for running or enforcing local programs
Foreign campaign money fine Misdemeanor with a fine equal to the amount given or spent Misdemeanor plus a fine of at least the amount and up to three times it
Changing the rules later Not applicable Definitions, spending-limit increases and the FPPC clause can be changed by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature that furthers the Political Reform Act; everything else needs voter approval
Compiled by California Today from the text of Proposition 4 (SB 42, Chapter 245 of 2025), the Legislative Analyst's analysis and the Assembly Elections Committee analysis of SB 42 (July 2, 2025). Dollar amounts, contribution matches and spending limits are not set by Proposition 4; each program would set its own.
The Fair Political Practices Commission would advise on Prop 4 programs but would not enforce local ones:
The FPPC, which enforces the Political Reform Act today, gets a limited role. The text says the commission "is not responsible for the administration or enforcement of a system of public funding of candidates established by a local governmental agency." The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm) expects state and local officials to ask the commission how to design programs that fit the new rules, which "likely would require the Fair Political Practices Commission to hire more legal staff." The FPPC told the Legislature it would need one attorney at a cost of $205,000 in the first year and $198,000 a year after that, according to the Assembly Elections Committee's analysis of SB 42 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/media/2586), and noted possible additional enforcement costs.
The measure also splits how its own rules can be changed later. The definitions, the spending-limit formula and the FPPC clause can be amended by the Legislature under the Political Reform Act's usual standard, a two-thirds vote in each house for a change that furthers the act's purposes. Every other part of the new section 85300, including the earmark exclusion and the ban on using public funds for fines and loan repayment, could be changed only with voters' approval.
Prop 4 also amends section 85320, the state's ban on contributions and spending by foreign governments, foreign principals and foreign nationals in state and local elections. Violating it is a misdemeanor today with a fine equal to the amount given or spent. Under Prop 4 the fine would be at least that amount and up to three times it. The committee analysis notes that this misdemeanor, unlike the act's general criminal penalty, does not require proof that a violation was knowing or willful.
California's ban on public campaign funds dates to Proposition 73 in 1988:
The ban came out of a head-to-head contest. In June 1988, voters faced two initiatives that would have rewritten campaign finance law in opposite directions. Proposition 68 offered contribution limits and state matching funds for legislative candidates who accepted spending limits. Proposition 73 offered contribution limits and a flat prohibition: "No public officer shall expend and no candidate shall accept any public money for the purpose of seeking elective office." Both passed, Prop 68 with 52.8% and Prop 73 with 58%, according to the Secretary of State's records (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/approval-percentages-initiatives.pdf). Because they conflicted, the California Supreme Court held in 1990 that only the measure with more yes votes could take effect, and Prop 68 was voided.
Federal courts later struck down Prop 73's contribution limits, but the public-funding ban survived. In 2000, voters approved Proposition 34, a Legislature-written campaign finance measure whose title promised contribution limits "Without Taxpayer Financing"; its ballot argument told voters that "our tax money is better spent on schools, roads and public safety."
The ban has one large exception. In 1992, in Johnson v. Bradley, the California Supreme Court upheld a Los Angeles charter measure that partly funded campaigns for city office, under the home-rule provision of the state Constitution. A 1990 appellate ruling held that the ban still applies to charter counties. The result, as the Assembly Elections Committee summarized it, is that "general law cities, all counties, all districts, and the state government are covered by the current ban," while charter cities can fund campaigns if they choose.
Three earlier measures to lift California's public financing ban failed between 2000 and 2010:
Each earlier attempt bundled the repeal with a specific program. Proposition 25 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2000-primary/sum_measures.pdf) in March 2000 would have publicly funded campaign advertising and voter information for candidates and ballot committees that accepted spending limits; it drew 34.7%. Proposition 89 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2006-general/measures.pdf) in November 2006 would have created a public financing system for candidates for state office; it drew 25.7%, the lowest of the three. Proposition 15 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2010-primary/ssov/ballot-measures-summary.pdf) in June 2010, placed on the ballot by the Legislature, would have run a public financing pilot for Secretary of State races; it drew 42.7%.
Prop 4 is built differently. It asks voters only to remove the ban and set conditions, and it leaves the decision to start a program, and how to pay for it, to each government.
SB 1107's 2016 attempt to lift the ban without a vote was struck down in court:
The Legislature has tried to remove the ban without a statewide vote before. In 2016 it passed SB 1107, by Senator Ben Allen, and Governor Jerry Brown signed it. The bill rewrote section 85300 to allow public funding when a government set up a dedicated fund open to all qualified candidates regardless of party or incumbency. Because Prop 73 had made the ban part of the voter-approved Political Reform Act, the Legislature could amend it without a vote only if the change furthered the act's purposes, and SB 1107 declared that it did.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and former Senator Quentin Kopp, one of Prop 73's proponents, sued. A Sacramento judge invalidated the law, and on August 26, 2019 the Third District Court of Appeal affirmed (https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) the judgment, finding that SB 1107 "directly conflicts with a primary purpose and mandate of the Act, as amended by subsequent voter initiatives, to prohibit public funding of political campaigns." The judgment bars the FPPC from enforcing it. SB 1107's wording stayed in the code, but the FPPC continues to enforce the ban. Prop 4 deletes that wording and replaces it, which is why it needs voters' approval to take effect.
Two earlier versions of the current measure, AB 270 and SB 24 in the 2023–24 session, died in the appropriations committees. SB 42 was introduced on December 5, 2024 and passed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) the Senate 28–10 on June 2, 2025. The Assembly passed it 59–20 on September 12, the Senate concurred 29–8 the next day, and Newsom signed it on October 2 as Chapter 245 of the Statutes of 2025.
Los Angeles, San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland already fund campaigns under the charter-city exception:
The Assembly Elections Committee counts at least seven charter cities with public financing programs: Berkeley, Long Beach, Los Angeles, Oakland, Richmond, Sacramento and San Francisco, though Richmond's and Sacramento's were not funded for recent elections. Most use matching funds, where the city multiplies small contributions from residents. Oakland's voters chose vouchers instead.
Four California charter cities fund campaigns with public money:
City Program and origin How candidates qualify What candidates can receive
Los Angeles Matching funds, enacted by city voters At least 100 contributions of $5 or more from district residents, at least $12,857 in qualified contributions, a $40,000 cap on self-funding, spending limits and a debate or town hall (2024 council rules) $6 for every $1 of a qualified contribution, matched up to $129 per donor; up to $174,000 in the primary and $217,000 in the general for a council candidate (2024)
San Francisco Public financing, created by Proposition O in November 2000 Supervisor candidates who are not incumbents need 100 resident contributions of $10 to $100 totaling $10,000; mayoral candidates who are not incumbents need 500 totaling $50,000; spending limits and three debates An initial grant, then $6 for every $1 raised; up to $255,000 for supervisor and $1.2 million for mayor (incumbents slightly less)
Berkeley Berkeley Fair Elections Act, approved by voters in 2016 At least 30 contributions of $10 or more from Berkeley residents totaling at least $650; a $60 cap on any one contribution and no loans (2026 rules) $6 for every $1 on contributions of up to $60; capped at $52,000 for City Council and $155,000 for mayor
Oakland Democracy Dollars, created by Measure W in November 2022 Candidates who opt in can collect vouchers from residents Each eligible resident gets $100 in vouchers to assign; the program is not funded for 2026 and is being prepared for 2028, with a limited public financing program in place for 2026
Compiled by California Today from the Los Angeles City Ethics Commission's 2024 Matching Funds FAQ, the San Francisco Ethics Commission's program overview, Berkeley's 2026 Public Financing Program guide and the Oakland Public Ethics Commission's Democracy Dollars page. Long Beach, Richmond and Sacramento have also enacted programs; the Assembly Elections Committee reports Richmond's and Sacramento's were not funded for recent elections.
San Francisco's program shows what one of these costs. City law requires a General Fund appropriation of $2.75 per resident each year into the Election Campaign Fund, capped at a $7 million balance. In the November 2024 mayoral and supervisorial races, the program paid out a record $8,840,187 to 27 candidates, $4.1 million of it to four mayoral candidates, according to the San Francisco Ethics Commission's post-election report (https://sfethics.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/2025.03.14-Agenda-Item-6-2024-Post-Election-Report.pdf). The same report found that outside groups spent $19.0 million on those races, also a record. Oakland shows the other side of the ledger: voters approved its $100-per-resident Democracy Dollars (https://www.oaklandca.gov/Government/Boards-Commissions/Public-Ethics-Commission/Democracy-Dollars-Program) program in November 2022, and the city has not funded it for 2026.
Proposition 4 costs the state a few hundred thousand dollars a year and leaves program costs to local choices:
The LAO's estimate covers only the state's direct cost: the FPPC's added legal staff, "much less than one-tenth of 1 percent" of the General Fund. Anything larger depends on what governments do afterward. "The cost of these programs could be significant for governments that choose to create them," the analysis says, and "the total cost would depend on which governments created such programs and how those programs were designed." Prop 4 does not require any government to create a program, and it does not say where the money would come from beyond excluding the three earmarked categories.
The two sides frame that open question differently. The Yes argument says that if a community adopts a program, "the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year." San Francisco law sets aside $2.75 per resident a year. The No argument says the measure "has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can receive"; the text indeed sets no dollar amount and leaves it to each program, which must also impose spending limits on the candidates it funds.
The Prop 4 campaign has raised $235,157 with no opposition committee:
Prop 4 is one of the quietest campaigns on the ballot. The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-4-sb-42-umberg-political-reform-act-1974-public-campaign-financing-california-fair-elections-act-2026-ch-245-2025), which runs through October 6, lists one committee, Movement Voter PAC's committee supporting Prop 4, with $235,157, and "No committees identified" in opposition. No committee on either side has raised the $1 million that puts it on the FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), last updated October 14. The Voter Information Guide lists the Yes campaign as Californians for Fair Elections, sponsored by Government Reform Advocates, and the No contact as the California Taxpayers Association.
The arguments on Proposition 4 split over special-interest money and taxpayer cost:
The argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California, Catherine Kennedy of the California Nurses Association and Senator Umberg, is headed "Elections should be won, not bought." It says "more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone" since 2020, that "thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems," and that Prop 4 "does not create a public financing program." Its rebuttal adds that "California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns."
The argument against, signed by former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, former FPPC commissioner Colleen McAndrews and Julian Canete of the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, says the measure "allows politicians to use your taxpayer money to fund their campaigns." It says Prop 4 sets "NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get," quotes the measure's definition of strict criteria to argue that "there is no current statute, ordinance or charter setting any criteria," and says candidates "can raise money from special interests AND get public funding too." Its rebuttal, signed by Robert Gutierrez of the California Taxpayers Association, Jon Coupal of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and Schnur, points to "more than 60 candidates" for governor in the June primary. The guide notes that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
The guide's index lists the League of Women Voters, the California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy, Social Security Works and Consumer Watchdog as supporters, and the California Taxpayers Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and United Latinos Action as opponents. In its letter to the Legislature, the California Taxpayers Association also raised a First Amendment objection, arguing that taxpayers "would be forced to finance political speech they do not wish to support."
Campaign voices on both sides have made the same points to reporters. Trent Lange, president of the California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes campaign, said candidates should be able "to run and win without having to raise big money," and Dora Rose of the League of Women Voters said Prop 4 "sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence," CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-proposition-4-explainer/). Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican, said on the Assembly floor that "the voters have been quite clear they don't want taxpayer money being used for politics." CalMatters also cites a National Conference of State Legislatures count of 15 states and Washington, D.C. with some form of statewide public financing, and describes the research on whether such programs reduce donors' influence as mixed.
Proposition 4 trails 42% to 53% in PPIC polling with Newsom and Democrats in support:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 42% yes, 53% no and 5% undecided, making Prop 4 one of the weakest measures on the ballot. Republicans oppose it 78% to 19% and independents 54% to 41%, while Democrats support it 55% to 39%. Self-described liberals back it 62% to 34%. Renters split 50% yes to 48% no while homeowners oppose it 55% to 39%, and households earning under $40,000 lean yes, 50% to 46%. One percent of likely voters named it the measure they are most interested in. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies, polling September 15–20, found 35% yes and 35% no with the rest undecided. PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.
Governor Newsom included a yes on Prop 4 in the ballot slate he announced on October 9. The California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) supports it and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) opposes it. Among editorial boards, the Sacramento Bee recommends yes and the San Diego Union-Tribune, the Orange County Register and the San Francisco Chronicle recommend no, according to CalMatters' roster (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/). The Chronicle argued that the measure's rules "are only meaningful if they're enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be." The Union-Tribune called Prop 4's "only certain effect" the creation of "a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for."
Proposition 4 after November 3 would hand the public financing decision to each government:
If Prop 4 passes, nothing changes on election day. The ban would end for the state, counties, general law cities and special districts, and any of them could then propose a program through its own statute, ordinance or charter, deciding the matching rate or voucher amount, the spending limits and the budget, within the measure's conditions. The FPPC would field questions, and a local program would be policed by whatever body that government sets up. Charter cities that already run programs would keep them. If it fails, the 1988 ban stays in place outside charter cities, as it has through three earlier repeal attempts and one struck-down law.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the text of SB 42 (Chapter 245, Statutes of 2025), campaign-finance data as of October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State) and October 14, 2026 (FPPC), party and candidate positions as of October 18, 2026, and polling fielded September 4–20, 2026.

Now I have a very complete picture. Let me also verify one more critical thing: the claim in the "Against" argument that Prop 4 "allows special interest money in politics" — i.e., candidates could take public funds AND big private contributions. Let me verify whether the measure requires participating candidates to limit/reject large contributions. Looking at the text: no explicit prohibition on also raising private contributions. But participating candidates must accept expenditure limits, which effectively caps total spending. In practice, matching-fund programs (like LA/SF) allow private contributions subject to contribution limits, and matching amplifies small ones. That's standard for the "small-donor matching" model — which is precisely the design that has the best evidence (NYC, LA per the 2017 study, though the study says LA's design was less effective than NYC's).

So the "No" argument that it "allows special interest money" is technically true but somewhat misleading: all public financing models except full-grant "clean elections" models allow continued private contributions. The measure's design (small-dollar qualifying + expenditure limits) is the matching-fund model.

Another key question: is there a serious concern about the Legislature self-funding? Yes — Prop 4 permits the state itself to create a program by statute. That means legislators could vote to fund their own campaigns. That's a genuine conflict-of-interest concern. But it would require an appropriation and, for most parts, 2/3 vote to amend the section. Also they'd be accountable to voters.

Cost: LAO says state direct cost a few hundred thousand/year. Any program costs are opt-in by each government. So Prop 4 itself costs essentially nothing. This is a crucial point — the "blank check" framing is inaccurate as a matter of the measure's direct fiscal effect. The LAO, a nonpartisan fiscal authority, confirms: the measure creates no program and spends no money; only a few hundred thousand a year for FPPC guidance.

Now, weighing:

Arguments FOR a Yes vote:
1. It's permissive, not mandatory. Zero direct cost. It doesn't spend a single taxpayer dollar on campaigns by itself.
2. California is a national outlier — the only state with a blanket statutory ban (per Yes campaign; the LAO confirms the ban applies to most state/local offices).
3. The 1988 ban was enacted in a very different era (pre-Citizens United). Since Citizens United (2010), independent expenditures are unlimited and unmatchable by contribution limits. Public financing is one of the few remaining constitutional tools (Buckley v. Valeo explicitly endorsed public financing as furthering a significant government interest).
4. Empirical evidence: LA's 6:1 matching program produced candidates averaging ~6,600 contributions of ~$530 each vs. non-participants' ~560 contributions of ~$25,000 each (GAO). Seattle Democracy Vouchers: donors per race +350%, sub-$200 donations +270%, candidates +86%. NYC small-donor public financing helped elect the most diverse city council. SF Ethics Commission found increased uptake and third-party spending at near all-time lows.
5. Meaningful guardrails are included: no education/transportation/public-safety money; mandatory expenditure limits; small-donor qualifying (max $10 counted per donor); no legal defense fees or fines; no repayment of personal loans (ever, from any source — the Swalwell loophole); no incumbency or party discrimination.
6. It triples fines for illegal foreign campaign money — a genuine election-security improvement.
7. Endorsed by: Gov. Newsom, CA Democratic Party, League of Women Voters, Common Cause, Consumer Watchdog, CA Nurses Association, ACLU of Northern California, CA Labor Federation, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy boards, LA Times (Skelton), Bay Area Reporter, SPUR, and — notably — the SF Chronicle's own voter guide tool lists "Yes" (their editorial board said no, though).
8. Local control: any program would still need to be adopted locally — and in most cases would go to local voters as a charter amendment or tax measure. Voters retain the final say on spending.

Arguments FOR a No vote:
1. Design vagueness: no dollar amounts, no minimum meaningful spending caps, no required independent oversight body. The FPPC is explicitly exempted from administering/enforcing local programs, and local governments aren't required to create their own watchdog. SF Chronicle's point is well-taken — the Farrell case shows enforcement matters.
2. Evidence on whether public financing reduces big-money influence is mixed (GAO 2010 found no evidence of more candidates in AZ/ME; Oakland 2013 found no reduction in wealthy donor influence). Independent expenditures post-Citizens United swamp candidate-level funds — SF's 2024 record $8.8M in public funds vs. $19M in outside spending.
3. Cost: programs cost real money at a time of local budget stress. SF pays $8.8M per cycle. Oakland voters approved Democracy Dollars but the city hasn't funded it — showing either fiscal strain or poor follow-through.
4. Taxpayer compulsion: taxpayers fund speech they oppose (CalTax First Amendment objection). Counter: same is true of all public spending, and the Supreme Court has rejected compelled-speech challenges to public financing.
5. Voters have rejected repeal three times (2000: 34.7%, 2006: 25.7%, 2010: 42.7%) and current polling shows it losing (PPIC 42–53; Berkeley IGS 35–35 with 30% undecided; late Oct 41–35).
6. Legislature could self-fund — incumbents writing their own campaign subsidies.
7. Subdivision (f)'s spending-limit "trigger" resembles Arizona's scheme struck down in Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) — potential litigation risk. Mitigated by subdivision (i), which lets the Legislature amend (e), (f), and (h) by 2/3 vote.

Let me verify one more thing: the amendment standard. The californiatoday table says: "The definitions, the spending-limit formula and the FPPC clause can be amended by the Legislature under the Political Reform Act's usual standard, a two-thirds vote in each house... Every other part of the new section 85300, including the earmark exclusion and the ban on using public funds for fines and loan repayment, could be changed only with voters' approval."

Wait — the text says subdivision (i): "Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) of this section may be amended by statute pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 81012. The remaining subdivisions of this section may be amended only by a statute that complies with subdivision (b) of Section 81012."

Section 81012: (a) allows amendment by 2/3 of each house if it furthers the purposes of the act; (b) allows amendment by majority vote if approved by the voters... Let me check. Actually Gov Code 81012: "The provisions of this act may be amended by statute..." Hmm. Let me verify: Proposition 9 (1974) — the Political Reform Act — Article: "No amendment to this Act shall be effective unless approved by the voters, except that the Legislature may amend... by a two-thirds vote in each house if the amendment furthers the purposes of this Act." So (a) = 2/3 vote furthers purposes; (b) = voter approval. So subdivisions (e), (f), (h) can be fixed by 2/3 legislative vote; the rest needs voter approval. That's actually a well-designed feature — it locks in the taxpayer protections (earmark exclusion, no legal fees/fines/loan repayment, spending limits, neutrality) against simple-majority legislative dilution, while leaving technical definitions flexible.

Hmm, so actually this is a strength: the core safeguards can only be removed by the voters. Good.

Let me quickly verify 81012 to be accurate.

Also, let me check the LA Times editorial board's position on Prop 4 — the cityhallpass site said "We found no LA Times editorial board position." George Skelton personally said Yes. Let me confirm.

Let me also double-check the "Only state that bans public funding" claim and confirm there's no hidden mandate. And check the KQED voter guide for any additional analysis.

Let me do a couple more verification searches.

Proposition 4
Should state and local governments have the option to provide public funding for election campaigns?
The measure would allow any state or local government to set up a public financing program for election campaigns. Candidates would need to meet certain eligibility criteria and agree to spending limits. The funds could not be used for legal defense costs, fines or repayment of personal loans. Proposition 4 would repeal a 1988 ban on using taxpayer dollars for election campaigns. Currently, only charter cities and counties can bypass that ban.
Yes Argument
Elections shouldn’t be determined by who has the greatest personal wealth or access to special interests. This measure would fight the influence of corporate money and super PACs by giving communities the opportunity to explore public financing programs that can help women, people of color and working-class candidates run competitive campaigns. It’s nonpartisan and prohibits public financing programs from favoring incumbents or political parties.
No Argument
Taxpayer dollars should be used for public services — like schools, roads and libraries — not political campaigns. At a time when cities and counties need more revenue for essential services, public financing opens the door to wasted taxpayer money on candidates who may never appear on the ballot. The measure is written too broadly, leaving each government to set its own eligibility criteria and spending limits, making the system vulnerable to abuse.

content.thinking:
Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me do one final check: is there any concern about the measure's interaction with the county central committees? And let me verify the LA Times position. Also let me quickly check whether there is a "compelled speech" First Amendment concern that would invalidate the measure (CalTax raised it). Under Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Ass'n and other cases, government speech subsidies are generally not compelled speech by taxpayers. The Supreme Court has upheld public financing repeatedly (Buckley). So low legal risk to the core repeal.

Let me do one more check on the LA Times editorial board and one on whether any progressive/anti-money-in-politics group opposes.

Actually, I have enough. Let me consider one more important thing: the "60 candidates for governor" claim — under Prop 4, would every candidate get taxpayer money? No: candidates must meet "strict criteria" demonstrating broad-based support (e.g., small-dollar contributions/vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents). So the "thousands of candidates get taxpayer money" claim is overstated — qualifying thresholds would filter. LA's program requires 100+ contributions of $5+ and $12,857 in qualified contributions. SF requires 100 contributions of $10-$100 totaling $10,000 for supervisors. That's a real filter. The opponents' argument is somewhat misleading.

Also the "no limit on how much" claim — true that Prop 4 sets no dollar amounts, but it mandates expenditure limits, which is a cap on spending by participating candidates. And each program sets its own amounts, subject to local voters (charter amendments typically require voter approval; new taxes require voter approval).

One more consideration: Is there a risk that a future Legislature creates a self-funding program for state legislative races? Possible but: (a) it'd require appropriations in a tight budget, (b) it'd require 2/3 to amend the section (though creating a new fund is by statute — a simple majority appropriation... actually creating a dedicated fund by statute = majority vote; but appropriating money generally requires... a simple majority for the budget, 2/3 for taxes). Hmm, so a majority-vote statute could create a state program. But that's exactly what "local control/democratic accountability" means. And notably, the Democratic supermajority could have created a state program — they haven't proposed one. SB 42 was purely enabling.

Let me also weigh: What is the actual expected effect? The most likely outcomes: more cities/counties (especially in the Bay Area and LA County) adopt matching-fund programs. Costs would be borne by those localities' voters who choose them. Downside risk: some poorly designed programs with weak oversight. Upside: expanded candidate pools, more small donors, less reliance on megadonors.

Given:
- The measure itself spends nothing (LAO-confirmed).
- It's purely permissive and preserves local democratic choice.
- It contains real, voter-locked safeguards (education/transportation/public safety money protected; no legal fees/fines/personal loan repayment; mandatory expenditure limits; small-donor qualifying capped at $10/donor; no incumbency or party discrimination).
- Those safeguards can only be weakened by a 2/3 legislative vote or the voters themselves.
- It triples penalties for illegal foreign money in California elections — a genuine election-security upgrade.
- Post-Citizens United, public financing is one of the few constitutionally viable tools left to counter unlimited independent spending; California is the only state that forecloses it entirely.
- Strong evidence from matching-fund and voucher programs (LA, Seattle, NYC) that they dramatically broaden the donor base and candidate pool — precisely the "special interest" problem voters say they care about (85% in Pew).

Against:
- Weak/absent mandated independent oversight of local programs (the strongest substantive criticism).
- Mixed evidence on whether it actually reduces big-money influence; independent expenditures dwarf candidate funds.
- Real costs if adopted, at a time of local budget strain.
- Vagueness leaves design to the politicians who benefit.

Weighing: The criticisms are about how well future programs might be designed — but those programs are opt-in and, in most jurisdictions, would require a local vote (charter amendments/taxes). The "No" campaign's core claims ("blank check," "thousands of candidates," "less money for schools") are directly contradicted by the LAO's analysis and the measure's text (which explicitly wall-offs education, transportation, and public safety money). The measure has essentially zero fiscal impact, expands local democratic choice, removes a 38-year-old outlier ban that predates Citizens United, and adds an election-security penalty.

The oversight gap is real but is a design flaw in a permissive statute that future programs can and should cure — and it's not a reason to permanently lock every non-charter city and county in California out of an option available in all 49 other states.

I'll vote YES.

Let me do one final verification search on the LA Times and any progressive opposition to make sure I'm not missing something significant. Actually, let me do one quick check for any news about a lawsuit or a serious problem discovered late.

## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns.*** The Political Reform Act bans the use of public funds for political candidates’ campaigns.
This ban applies to most elected offices at the state level and local level.
(This ban does not apply to city office elections in certain charter cities.
Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley are current examples of charter cities that provide public funds to certain campaigns.)
...
### Proposal
***Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates’ Campaigns.*** Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates’ campaigns.
Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish.
Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
***Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs.*** Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers.
Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program.
For example, money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns.

1. **What it is**: Prop 4 (SB 42, Umberg, Ch. 245 of 2025), the California Fair Elections Act of 2026. Repeals Government Code §85300's blanket ban on public campaign financing (from Prop 73, 1988) and replaces it with conditional permission. Also triples fines for illegal foreign campaign money (§85320).

2. **Fiscal impact**: LAO — no program created, no money spent. State cost: "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for FPPC guidance (FPPC asked for ~$205K first year, $198K/yr after). Less than 0.1% of the General Fund. Local costs only if a government opts in.

3. **Guardrails in the text**:
   - Money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used.
   - Participating candidates must accept expenditure limits.
   - Must demonstrate broad-based support via small-dollar contributions/vouchers; max countable contribution $10.
   - No public funds for legal defense fees or fines.
   - No repayment of personal campaign loans from public funds — ever, from any source, even after the campaign ends.
   - Programs may not discriminate by party or incumbency; funds available to all qualified candidates for the same office.
   - Amendment protection: subdivisions (e), (f), (h) amendable by 2/3 legislature; ALL OTHER subdivisions (including the earmark protection, expenditure limits, legal-fee/loan bans, neutrality) require voter approval under §81012(b). So the core taxpayer protections are locked in against simple-majority legislative dilution.

4. **Context**: California is the only state with a blanket statutory ban (Johnson v. Bradley (1992) carved out charter cities only). 15 states + DC and ~26 localities have programs. The ban predates Citizens United (2010) by 22 years — it was written for a world where contribution limits could actually constrain campaign money. Now unlimited independent expenditures are the dominant force; Buckley v. Valeo affirmed public financing "furthers a significant governmental interest."

5. **Evidence**: Mixed but with strong positives on the specific outcomes that matter:
   - LA 2022 mayoral: publicly financed candidates averaged ~6,600 contributions of ~$530; non-participants ~560 contributions of ~$25,000 (GAO).
   - Seattle Democracy Vouchers: donors per race +350%, sub-$200 donations +270%, candidates +86%; voucher users ~12x more likely to vote; low-income residents and people of color more likely to use vouchers.
   - Berkeley after 2018: non-resident contributions fell from 33% to 10%.
   - NYC small-donor matching helped elect the most diverse city council.
   - GAO (2025): publicly financed candidates won/advanced in ≥50% of contests in 4 of 5 studied jurisdictions.
   - Counter-evidence: GAO 2010 found no increase in candidates in AZ/ME; Oakland 2013 found no reduction in wealthy-donor influence; a 2017 peer-reviewed study found LA's program design "substantially less effective" than NYC's; little evidence public financing curbs overall private-donor influence.
   
   Honest read: design matters enormously. Programs with high match rates + low qualifying thresholds + vouchers work; poorly designed ones don't.

6. **Weaknesses of Prop 4** (the strongest genuine criticisms):
   - Explicitly exempts FPPC from administering/enforcing local programs, and does NOT require local governments to create an independent oversight body. The SF Chronicle's Mark Farrell example is a fair illustration of why enforcement matters.
   - No mandated design standards (match rates, qualifying thresholds, minimum meaningful spending caps), so a jurisdiction could adopt an ineffective or self-serving program.
   - Legislature could theoretically create a state program funding its own campaigns.
   - Subdivision (f)'s spending-limit escalation formula resembles Arizona's matching-funds trigger struck down in Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) — litigation risk. (Mitigated: (f) is amendable by 2/3 legislature.)

7. **Weaknesses of the "No" case**:

   - "Thousands of candidates get taxpayer money" — contradicted by the mandatory "strict criteria" showing broad-based support (real programs require 100+ resident small-dollar contributions, e.g., LA and SF).
   - "No limit on how much" — true that Prop 4 sets no dollar figure, but it mandates that participating candidates accept expenditure limits.
   - "Allows special interest money" — technically true but this describes virtually every matching-fund program in the country (NYC, LA, Seattle, Berkeley); only full-grant "clean elections" models forbid private money, and those are the ones the GAO found least effective at generating candidates.

   - The "No" side raised $0 (no opposition committee registered at all through Oct 22), while Yes raised ~$992K from CNA-PAC, Movement Voter PAC, an individual, the CA Labor Federation, and ACLU NorCal — i.e., the opposition is not funded by threatened special interests either. Notably, no business/corporate money organized against it. This is a low-money, low-salience measure (1% of voters named it the measure they most care about).

8. **Endorsements**:

Newsom, CA Democratic Party, League of Women Voters, CA Common Cause, Consumer Watchdog, CA Nurses Association, ACLU NorCal, CA Labor Federation, Sacramento Bee + McClatchy CA boards (Modesto, Merced, Fresno, SLO Tribune), LA Times (Skelton; no formal board position), Bay Area Reporter, SPUR.
   - NO: CA Republican Party, CalTax, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn, Reform California/DeMaio, Family Business Assn, United Latinos Action, CA Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, SF Chronicle, SDUT, OC Register/SCNG papers (Daily News, Record-Bee), Mercury News/East Bay Times, Press Democrat; Santa Cruz Sentinel neutral; former FPPC chair Dan Schnur and former commissioner Colleen McAndrews.

Now, the decision.

The decisive analytical points for me:

**A. The measure's own cost and effect are minimal and well-defined.** This is not a spending measure. The LAO — the most trusted nonpartisan fiscal referee in California — says it creates no program, spends no campaign money, and costs the state a few hundred thousand dollars a year. The "blank check" framing fails on the LAO's own analysis. Voting "no" doesn't save taxpayers anything; it just forecloses an option.

**B. Voting yes preserves democratic choice; voting no removes it permanently for most Californians.** The status quo is that 480+ cities, all 58 counties, all districts, and the state itself are barred — an artifact of a 1988 vote taken in a pre-Citizens United world. California is the sole state with a blanket ban. Prop 4 doesn't force anything on anyone; it hands the decision to each community, and in practice most such programs require a local charter amendment or tax vote — meaning local voters still get the final say on any actual spending. If a program is bad, local voters can kill it. That's a strictly more democratic position than a permanent statewide prohibition.

**C. The safeguards are real and unusually well-locked.** Education/transportation/public-safety money is protected; expenditure limits are mandatory; qualifying must be small-dollar (max $10 countable per donor); no legal-defense fees, no fines, no personal-loan repayment ever; no incumbency or party favoritism. Critically, under §81012(b), those protections can be stripped only by the voters themselves — not by a simple legislative majority. That's a better anti-abuse design than most statutes.

**D. The oversight gap is real but is not a reason for a permanent ban.** The SF Chronicle's criticism — that Prop 4 exempts the FPPC and doesn't require a local watchdog — is the most substantive objection, and I take it seriously. But the remedy is for adopting jurisdictions to build oversight (as SF, LA, Berkeley, Oakland all have: ethics commissions), and for the Legislature to require it. That's a fixable design problem in an opt-in statute, not a justification for locking every non-charter community in California out of an option available in all 49 other states forever.

**E. The problem being addressed is real and worsening.** Over $1 billion spent on state candidate races since 2020; the most expensive governor's race in US history (Steyer's $213M self-funding); a billionaire-backed PAC spending ~$250M this cycle; 85% of Americans say campaign costs deter good people from running. Post-Citizens United, contribution limits can no longer contain the money — public financing is one of the few constitutionally permissible tools remaining (Buckley explicitly blessed it). And the best evidence on well-designed programs is genuinely encouraging: LA's 2022 publicly financed candidates averaged ~6,600 donations of ~$530 versus ~560 donations of ~$25,000 for non-participants; Seattle's vouchers raised candidates 86% and donors 350%; Berkeley cut non-resident money from 33% to 10%.

**F. The measure also does something unambiguously good:** it triples the penalties for illegal foreign-government/foreign-national money in California elections — an election-security upgrade with no downside.

**G. The "mixed evidence" objection cuts both ways but favors yes here.** The negative studies (GAO 2010 on AZ/ME, Oakland 2013, the LA-vs-NYC design study) show that badly designed programs underperform — which is an argument for designing well, not for banning. And a permissive statute is exactly the vehicle for experimentation: it lets jurisdictions learn from SF/LA/Berkeley/Seattle/NYC and adopt what works. A "no" vote guarantees California never learns anything, while keeping the outlier ban in place.

Counterweight I have to be honest about: this measure polls badly (PPIC 42–53; Berkeley IGS 35–35 with 30% undecided, then 41–35), it has failed three prior times (34.7%, 25.7%, 42.7%), and voters have a durable, legitimate aversion to politicians self-funding. And a Legislature with a supermajority did vote to enable a mechanism that could, in principle, benefit incumbents. Those are real. But my job is to assess the merits, not the polling — and on the merits, the measure costs essentially nothing, spends nothing itself, contains voter-locked safeguards, protects school/road/police money by name, expands rather than restricts local democratic choice, and removes a 38-year-old outlier prohibition that predates the post-Citizens United money flood it was meant to address.

The downside risk is bounded and reversible (local voters can repeal a bad local program). The downside of "no" is permanent and statewide (the ban stays, and only a future ballot measure can lift it).

   - "No limit on how much" — true that Prop 4 sets no dollar figure, but it mandates that participating candidates accept expenditure limits.
   - "Allows special interest money" — technically true but this describes virtually every matching-fund program in the country (NYC, LA, Seattle, Berkeley); only full-grant "clean elections" models forbid private money, and those are the ones the GAO found least effective at generating candidates.
   - SDUT's argument that the five charter cities with programs are "poorly run" is an unsupported ad hominem, not an analysis of the programs.
   - The "No" side raised $0 (no opposition committee registered at all through Oct 22), while Yes raised ~$992K from CNA-PAC, Movement Voter PAC, an individual, the CA Labor Federation, and ACLU NorCal — i.e., the opposition is not funded by threatened special interests either. Notably, no business/corporate money organized against it. This is a low-money, low-salience measure (1% of voters named it the measure they most care about).

8. **Endorsements**: 
   - YES: Gov. Newsom, CA Democratic Party, League of Women Voters, CA Common Cause, Consumer Watchdog, CA Nurses Association, ACLU NorCal, CA Labor Federation, Sacramento Bee + McClatchy CA boards (Modesto, Merced, Fresno, SLO Tribune), LA Times (Skelton; no formal board position), Bay Area Reporter, SPUR.
   - NO: CA Republican Party, CalTax, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn, Reform California/DeMaio, Family Business Assn, United Latinos Action, CA Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, SF Chronicle, SDUT, OC Register/SCNG papers (Daily News, Record-Bee), Mercury News/East Bay Times, Press Democrat; Santa Cruz Sentinel neutral; former FPPC chair Dan Schnur and former commissioner Colleen McAndrews.

Now, the decision.

The decisive analytical points for me:

**A. The measure's own cost and effect are minimal and well-defined.** This is not a spending measure. The LAO — the most trusted nonpartisan fiscal referee in California — says it creates no program, spends no campaign money, and costs the state a few hundred thousand dollars a year. The "blank check" framing fails on the LAO's own analysis. Voting "no" doesn't save taxpayers anything; it just forecloses an option.

**B. Voting yes preserves democratic choice; voting no removes it permanently for most Californians.** The status quo is that 480+ cities, all 58 counties, all districts, and the state itself are barred — an artifact of a 1988 vote taken in a pre-Citizens United world. California is the sole state with a blanket ban. Prop 4 doesn't force anything on anyone; it hands the decision to each community, and in practice most such programs require a local charter amendment or tax vote — meaning local voters still get the final say on any actual spending. If a program is bad, local voters can kill it. That's a strictly more democratic position than a permanent statewide prohibition.

**C. The safeguards are real and unusually well-locked.** Education/transportation/public-safety money is protected; expenditure limits are mandatory; qualifying must be small-dollar (max $10 countable per donor); no legal-defense fees, no fines, no personal-loan repayment ever; no incumbency or party favoritism. Critically, under §81012(b), those protections can be stripped only by the voters themselves — not by a simple legislative majority. That's a better anti-abuse design than most statutes.

**D. The oversight gap is real but is not a reason for a permanent ban.** The SF Chronicle's criticism — that Prop 4 exempts the FPPC and doesn't require a local watchdog — is the most substantive objection, and I take it seriously. But the remedy is for adopting jurisdictions to build oversight (as SF, LA, Berkeley, Oakland all have: ethics commissions), and for the Legislature to require it. That's a fixable design problem in an opt-in statute, not a justification for locking every non-charter community in California out of an option available in all 49 other states forever.

**E. The problem being addressed is real and worsening.** Over $1 billion spent on state candidate races since 2020; the most expensive governor's race in US history (Steyer's $213M self-funding); a billionaire-backed PAC spending ~$250M this cycle; 85% of Americans say campaign costs deter good people from running. Post-Citizens United, contribution limits can no longer contain the money — public financing is one of the few constitutionally permissible tools remaining (Buckley explicitly blessed it). And the best evidence on well-designed programs is genuinely encouraging: LA's 2022 publicly financed candidates averaged ~6,600 donations of ~$530 versus ~560 donations of ~$25,000 for non-participants; Seattle's vouchers raised candidates 86% and donors 350%; Berkeley cut non-resident money from 33% to 10%.

**F. The measure also does something unambiguously good:** it triples the penalties for illegal foreign-government/foreign-national money in California elections — an election-security upgrade with no downside.

**G. The "mixed evidence" objection cuts both ways but favors yes here.** The negative studies (GAO 2010 on AZ/ME, Oakland 2013, the LA-vs-NYC design study) show that badly designed programs underperform — which is an argument for designing well, not for banning. And a permissive statute is exactly the vehicle for experimentation: it lets jurisdictions learn from SF/LA/Berkeley/Seattle/NYC and adopt what works. A "no" vote guarantees California never learns anything, while keeping the outlier ban in place.

Counterweight I have to be honest about: this measure polls badly (PPIC 42–53; Berkeley IGS 35–35 with 30% undecided, then 41–35), it has failed three prior times (34.7%, 25.7%, 42.7%), and voters have a durable, legitimate aversion to politicians self-funding. And a Legislature with a supermajority did vote to enable a mechanism that could, in principle, benefit incumbents. Those are real. But my job is to assess the merits, not the polling — and on the merits, the measure costs essentially nothing, spends nothing itself, contains voter-locked safeguards, protects school/road/police money by name, expands rather than restricts local democratic choice, and removes a 38-year-old outlier prohibition that predates the post-Citizens United money flood it was meant to address.

The downside risk is bounded and reversible (local voters can repeal a bad local program). The downside of "no" is permanent and statewide (the ban stays, and only a future ballot measure can lift it).

I vote YES.

**Yes.**

---

**What it actually is** (note: this is the Nov 3, **2026** ballot — Prop 4 here is SB 42/Ch. 245 of 2025, the "California Fair Elections Act," not the 2024 climate bond). It repeals the 1988 Prop 73 blanket ban on public campaign financing (Gov. Code §85300) and replaces it with conditional permission. It creates no program and appropriates nothing. It also triples fines for illegal foreign campaign money.

**Why yes:**

- **It costs essentially nothing.** The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst confirms no program is created and no campaign money is spent; state cost is "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for FPPC guidance — under 0.1% of the General Fund. Local costs arise only if a government opts in, and in practice via a charter amendment or tax vote, so local voters still get final say on any real spending.
- **The "blank check / less money for schools" attack is contradicted by the text and the LAO.** Education, transportation, and public-safety money is explicitly walled off. Expenditure limits are *mandatory*. Qualifying must be small-dollar (no contribution over $10 can be required to count). Public funds can never pay legal defense fees, fines, or repay a candidate's personal loan — ever, from any source.
- **The safeguards are unusually well-locked.** Under Gov. Code §81012(b), those protections can be stripped only by the voters, not by a simple legislative majority. Only the technical definitions/escalation formula/FPPC clause are 2/3-amendable.
- **California is the sole state with a blanket ban** — an artifact of 1988, 22 years pre-*Citizens United*. With unlimited independent spending now dominant, small-donor public financing is one of the few constitutionally viable tools left (*Buckley*: it "furthers a significant governmental interest"). $1B+ spent on state candidate races since 2020; the most expensive governor's race in U.S. history.
- **The best-designed programs show real results.** LA 2022: publicly financed candidates averaged ~6,600 contributions of ~$530 vs. ~560 of ~$25,000 for non-participants (GAO). Seattle vouchers: candidates +86%, donors per race +350%, voucher users far likelier to vote. Berkeley: non-resident money fell 33%→10%. GAO found publicly financed candidates won/advanced in ≥50% of contests in 4 of 5 jurisdictions studied.
- **Voting no is the irreversible choice.** A bad local program can be repealed locally. A "no" keeps a permanent statewide prohibition that only another ballot measure can lift — and guarantees California never learns from its own experiments.

**The strongest honest objection** (SF Chronicle): Prop 4 exempts the FPPC from enforcing local programs and doesn't require an independent local watchdog, and it sets no design standards — the Mark Farrell SF case shows enforcement matters. That's a real flaw. But it's a fixable design gap in an *opt-in* statute, not a reason to permanently exclude every non-charter city, all 58 counties, all districts and the state from an option available in all 49 other states.

Context worth knowing: it polls behind (PPIC 42–53; Berkeley IGS 35–35, later 41–35) and similar repeals failed in 2000, 2006 and 2010. The No side raised $0 with no registered committee; Yes raised ~$992K (nurses' union, Movement Voter PAC, labor federation, ACLU NorCal). Backed by Newsom, League of Women Voters, Common Cause, Consumer Watchdog, the McClatchy California boards and SPUR; opposed by CalTax, Howard Jarvis, Reform California, the Chronicle, the Union-Tribune and SCNG papers.
